title: Honor and Shame
summary: In the biblical world a person's worth was largely a public matter: honor was reputation granted by the community, and shame was its loss. Many gospel scenes are contests over honor that a modern reader can miss.
body:
Ancient Mediterranean societies, Israelite, Greek and Roman alike, were what anthropologists call honor-shame cultures. Honor was the public recognition of a person's claim to worth, and it came in two forms: ascribed honor, inherited through birth, family and office, and acquired honor, won through benefaction, wisdom, courage or success in public challenges. Because honor was thought of as limited, one person's gain was often another's loss, and families guarded it collectively. Proverbs can say that a good name is to be chosen rather than great riches (Prov 22:1), and God says through the man of God to Eli that those who honor him he will honor, while those who despise him will be lightly esteemed (1 Sam 2:30).

Much public life ran on a pattern of challenge and riposte. A question put to a teacher in public, such as the Pharisees' and Herodians' question about tribute or the Sadducees' question about the resurrection, was a challenge to his honor; a clever answer that silenced the questioners won honor for him and shamed them (Mark 12:13-27; Matt 22:46). Seating at banquets displayed rank, which is why Jesus advises taking the lowest place so that the host may say 'Friend, move up higher' (Luke 14:7-11). A prophet was without honor in his hometown because the village already 'knew' his ascribed status as the carpenter's son (Mark 6:3-4).

This background sharpens several texts. The father in the parable of the lost son behaves shamefully by local standards when he runs to meet his son, and in doing so absorbs the son's disgrace in public (Luke 15:20-24). A slap on the right cheek, presumably with the back of the right hand, was an insult more than an injury, so turning the other cheek is about refusing the honor game (Matt 5:39). Jesus warns against doing righteous deeds to be seen by others (Matt 6:1-4) and asks how people can believe when they receive glory from one another (John 5:44).

Crucifixion was designed to be the ultimate public degradation, and Hebrews says Jesus endured the cross, despising the shame (Heb 12:2). Paul is not ashamed of the gospel (Rom 1:16) and builds a theology in which God has chosen what the world counts shameful to shame the wise (1 Cor 1:26-29). Some missiologists argue that Western theology has stressed guilt and legal categories while much of scripture also frames sin and salvation as dishonor and restored honor; others reply that the legal and relational categories belong together in the text itself.

title: Patronage and Benefaction
summary: The Roman world was held together by unequal but reciprocal relationships between patrons who gave protection, money or access and clients who returned loyalty, praise and service. The New Testament's vocabulary of grace, faith and thanks sits inside this world.
body:
In Roman society a patron (patronus) supplied what a client could not obtain alone: a loan, a job, legal protection, a recommendation, a seat at dinner, access to someone more powerful. The client (cliens) repaid with loyalty, public praise, votes and attendance; in the city of Rome clients gathered at a patron's door for the morning greeting (salutatio). Between cities and the wealthy the same logic appeared as benefaction (euergetism): rich citizens paid for buildings, games, grain or festivals and were honored with inscriptions, statues and titles such as 'benefactor'. Jesus alludes to this when he says the kings of the Gentiles are called benefactors (Luke 22:25).

The gospels show local versions of the system. Elders of Capernaum plead for a centurion because he loves the nation and built them a synagogue, the kind of benefaction that created an obligation (Luke 7:2-5). Pilate is pressured with the charge that releasing Jesus would mean he is not Caesar's friend, a phrase that may echo the formal status of 'friend of Caesar' (John 19:12). Brokers stood between patrons and clients, and the disciples sometimes act like brokers who control access to Jesus (Mark 10:13-14).

The vocabulary of gift exchange runs through the letters. *Charis* (grace) was the ordinary word for a benefactor's favor and for the gratitude it obliged; *pistis* (faith) could mean the loyalty a client owed. Paul calls Phoebe a *prostatis*, a patroness or benefactor of many including himself (Rom 16:1-2). Lydia opens her household to the missionaries (Acts 16:15). Paul thanks the Philippians for a gift while carefully refusing to be placed in their debt, presenting it instead as a sacrifice to God (Phil 4:10-19), and at Corinth he refuses support, partly to avoid becoming a dependent client of wealthy members (1 Cor 9:12-18).

Scholars such as John Barclay have argued that ancient gifts were rarely 'free' in the modern sense; they created relationships and expected return. Paul's distinctive claim was that God's gift in Christ was given to the unworthy without regard to prior worth (Rom 5:6-8) while still expecting a transformed life in response (Rom 12:1). How to describe that combination is part of the wider Protestant and Catholic discussion of grace and works.

title: Hospitality
summary: Hospitality to strangers was a sacred duty in the ancient Near East and a practical necessity for travelers. Scripture repeatedly turns it into a test of righteousness and a picture of God's welcome.
body:
In a world with few inns and dangerous roads, receiving strangers was both a moral obligation and a survival network. The pattern was well known: notice the traveler, invite him in, wash his feet, feed him generously, protect him while under your roof, and send him off safely. Abraham at Mamre runs to meet three strangers, has water brought for their feet and has a calf prepared, far more than the 'morsel of bread' he offers (Gen 18:1-8). Job lists hospitality among the marks of his integrity: the stranger did not lodge in the street (Job 31:32).

The host's duty of protection could be extreme. Lot shelters his guests in Sodom and is willing to sacrifice his daughters rather than hand them over (Gen 19:1-8), and the narrative of the Levite at Gibeah, where no one but an old outsider takes in the travelers, shows a society in collapse (Judg 19:15-21). Rahab's reception of the spies and her protection of them is remembered as faith in action (Josh 2:1-7; Heb 11:31; Jas 2:25). Israel's law grounds care for the sojourner in its own experience as strangers in Egypt (Lev 19:33-34).

In the gospels Jesus is often the guest, and the quality of hospitality becomes a sign. Simon the Pharisee omitted the water for feet, the kiss and the oil, while the sinful woman supplied them all (Luke 7:44-46). Jesus sends the seventy-two out dependent on hospitality, eating what is set before them (Luke 10:5-8), and Martha receives him in her home (Luke 10:38). Judgment itself turns on whether the stranger was welcomed (Matt 25:35-40).

The early church spread through households that hosted traveling missionaries and gatherings: Lydia (Acts 16:15), Priscilla and Aquila (Rom 16:3-5), Gaius (Rom 16:23). Believers are told to pursue hospitality (Rom 12:13), to offer it without grumbling (1 Pet 4:9), and to remember that some have entertained angels unawares, a clear echo of Abraham (Heb 13:2). Elders must be hospitable (1 Tim 3:2), and 3 John commends support of traveling teachers while 2 John warns against hosting those who deny the incarnation (3 John 1:5-8; 2 John 1:10-11).

facts.value: Invitation, foot-washing, meal, protection, safe send-off (Gen 18:1-8)

facts.value: Philoxenia, literally 'love of strangers' (Rom 12:13; Heb 13:2)

facts.value: Israel was itself a stranger in Egypt (Lev 19:34)

title: Kinship and Inheritance
summary: Israelite identity was nested in father's house, clan and tribe, and land passed down within the family as a trust from God. Redemption, adoption and inheritance language in scripture grows directly out of this system.
body:
An Israelite belonged first to a 'father's house' (*bet av*), an extended household of several generations under a senior male; then to a clan (*mishpachah*); then to a tribe (*shevet* or *matteh*). The selection of Achan moves through exactly these levels: tribe, clan, household, man (Josh 7:16-18). Genealogies were therefore not dry lists but statements of identity, land rights and status, which is why Ezra excludes priests who could not find their family records (Ezra 2:61-62) and why Matthew opens his gospel with Jesus' descent from Abraham and David (Matt 1:1-17).

Land belonged ultimately to God, and Israelites held it as tenants: the land shall not be sold in perpetuity (Lev 25:23). Naboth refuses to sell his vineyard to Ahab because it is the inheritance of his fathers (1 Kgs 21:3). Inheritance normally passed to sons, with the firstborn receiving a double portion even if he was the son of the less-loved wife (Deut 21:15-17). The daughters of Zelophehad successfully petitioned to inherit when there was no son, on condition that they marry within their tribe so that the land stayed put (Num 27:1-11; Num 36:6-9).

Two institutions protected the family line. The kinsman-redeemer (*go'el*) bought back land or relatives lost through debt (Lev 25:25; Lev 25:47-49) and avenged blood. Levirate marriage required a man to raise up a son for his dead brother (Deut 25:5-10). Both lie behind the stories of Tamar and Judah (Gen 38) and of Boaz, who acts as redeemer for Naomi's land and marries Ruth (Ruth 4:1-10). The patriarchal narratives also turn on birthright and blessing: Esau sells his birthright, Jacob takes the blessing (Gen 25:29-34; Gen 27).

The New Testament assumes this world. The younger son's demand for his share while his father lives is shocking (Luke 15:12), and a man asks Jesus to make his brother divide the inheritance (Luke 12:13-15). Paul uses Greco-Roman adoption, which made the adoptee a full heir with a new legal father, to describe believers as sons and heirs of God (Gal 4:1-7; Rom 8:15-17). Hebrews and Peter speak of an imperishable inheritance (Heb 9:15; 1 Pet 1:4). How the land promise to Abraham's family relates to this wider inheritance is a key question in discussions of Israel and the church.

title: Marriage and Family
summary: Marriage in the biblical world was a covenant between families as well as individuals, arranged by parents, sealed by betrothal and payments, and centered on producing heirs. Its customs explain betrothal, divorce debates and wedding imagery in scripture.
body:
Marriages were normally arranged by parents, often between related families, and girls typically married young, around their mid-teens, while men were often older. The groom or his family paid a bride-price (*mohar*) to the bride's father (Gen 34:12; Exod 22:16-17), sometimes in labor, as Jacob served seven years for Rachel (Gen 29:18-20); the bride brought a dowry, and fathers sometimes gave land or servants (Josh 15:18-19). The wife usually moved into her husband's father's household. Polygyny was permitted and practised, especially by patriarchs and kings, and the narratives show its jealousies frankly (Gen 30:1-24; 1 Sam 1:1-8).

Betrothal (*erusin*) was legally binding: a betrothed woman was called a wife, and unfaithfulness counted as adultery (Deut 22:23-24). This is why Joseph, betrothed to Mary, could only end the relationship by divorce (Matt 1:18-19). The wedding itself, often a year later in Jewish practice, involved the groom's procession to fetch the bride, a feast lasting up to seven days (Judg 14:12), and guests who were expected to be ready (Matt 25:1-13). Running out of wine at Cana would have been a real social embarrassment for the host family (John 2:1-11).

Deuteronomy regulates divorce by requiring a written certificate (Deut 24:1-4). In Jesus' day the schools of Shammai and Hillel disputed the phrase 'some indecency': Shammai limited it to sexual misconduct, Hillel allowed divorce for nearly any cause (later recorded in Mishnah Gittin 9:10). The Pharisees' question about divorce 'for any cause' enters this debate, and Jesus answers by appealing to creation (Matt 19:3-9; Gen 2:24). Malachi had already said that God hates divorce or, on another reading, that a man who divorces covers himself with violence (Mal 2:16).

Greco-Roman households were legally headed by the *paterfamilias*, and philosophers wrote 'household codes' on managing wife, children and slaves. The New Testament adopts the form but addresses each member as a moral agent and grounds it in Christ (Eph 5:21-6:9; Col 3:18-4:1; 1 Pet 3:1-7). How those codes apply today is central to the debate over gender roles. Scripture also uses marriage as a governing image for God and his people, from Hosea to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Hos 2:19-20; Eph 5:31-32; Rev 19:7-9).

title: Slavery in the Ancient World
summary: Slavery was woven into every ancient economy, though its forms differed: Israelite law mainly addressed debt-servitude with limits and release, while Roman slavery was large-scale chattel slavery with frequent manumission. Readers need both pictures to understand the biblical texts.
body:
In Israel most servitude arose from debt. A Hebrew who sold himself or was sold for debt served six years and went free in the seventh, and Deuteronomy requires the master to send him off liberally supplied (Exod 21:2-6; Deut 15:12-18). Leviticus frames such people as hired workers rather than slaves and permits permanent slavery only of foreigners (Lev 25:39-46). Laws also limited abuse: a slave who lost an eye or a tooth went free (Exod 21:26-27), kidnapping a person to sell was a capital crime (Exod 21:16), and runaway slaves were not to be returned to their masters (Deut 23:15-16), a striking contrast with Babylonian law. The prophets condemned Judah for re-enslaving released servants (Jer 34:8-17).

Roman slavery was on a different scale. Estimates vary, but slaves may have made up roughly 10 percent of the empire's population and perhaps 15 to 25 percent in Roman Italy. People became slaves through war, piracy, birth, exposure as infants and debt. Slaves worked in mines and on estates in brutal conditions, but also as household servants, teachers, doctors, secretaries and business managers. Masters held near-absolute legal power over them. Manumission was common in cities, often around age thirty, producing a large class of freedmen with obligations to their former owners.

The New Testament addresses this world directly. Paul tells slaves that if they can gain freedom they should take it (1 Cor 7:21-23), sends the runaway or estranged Onesimus back to Philemon as 'a beloved brother' and hints strongly at more (Phlm 1:15-21), and tells masters that they and their slaves share one Master in heaven (Eph 6:5-9; Col 4:1). He lists 'enslavers' among the lawless (1 Tim 1:10), and Revelation condemns Babylon for trading in 'bodies and souls of men' (Rev 18:13). In Christ there is neither slave nor free (Gal 3:28).

Paul and others call themselves 'slaves' (*douloi*) of Christ (Rom 1:1), and redemption language draws on the purchase or release of slaves (1 Cor 6:19-20; Gal 4:1-7). Christians have long disagreed about how far these texts accommodated an existing institution and how far they planted principles that would dismantle it; the same texts were cited both by defenders of American slavery and by abolitionists. Debates about how the New Testament's household codes apply today, including to gender, often turn on how this question is answered.

title: Women in the Ancient World
summary: Women in Israel, Judea and the Roman world mostly lived under male guardianship, yet scripture records women as prophets, judges, patrons, disciples and the first witnesses of the resurrection. The background clarifies both the constraints and the surprises.
body:
In ancient Israel a woman normally passed from her father's household to her husband's. Her vows could be annulled by father or husband (Num 30:3-16), and legal and inheritance rights mainly flowed through men, with exceptions such as the daughters of Zelophehad (Num 27:1-11). Yet women's work was economically central: spinning, weaving, food production, managing servants and, as Proverbs 31 shows, buying fields and trading (Prov 31:10-31). Some women held public religious and political authority: Miriam the prophetess (Exod 15:20-21), Deborah who judged Israel (Judg 4:4-5), and Huldah, whom King Josiah's officials consulted about the book of the law (2 Kgs 22:14-20).

In the first century the picture varied by region and class. Jewish women could own property, as marriage contracts and the Babatha archive from the early second century show. Josephus says women were not accepted as legal witnesses (*Antiquities* 4.219), and a court of women in Herod's temple marked the limit beyond which they could not go. Roman women of the elite could be wealthy and influential, often acting through a male guardian, and inscriptions show women as patrons of associations and synagogues.

Against this background the gospels stand out. Women travel with Jesus and support his mission from their own means (Luke 8:1-3). Mary of Bethany sits at his feet, the posture of a disciple (Luke 10:39). Jesus speaks publicly with a Samaritan woman, to his disciples' surprise (John 4:27). Women witness the crucifixion and burial and are the first witnesses of the empty tomb and the risen Jesus (Mark 15:40-47; Matt 28:1-10; John 20:11-18). Because women's testimony was devalued, many scholars argue the early church would not have invented this detail.

In Paul's churches women appear as patrons and co-workers: Phoebe the deacon or minister of Cenchreae (Rom 16:1-2), Priscilla who with Aquila taught Apollos (Acts 18:26), Junia 'outstanding among the apostles' (Rom 16:7), Euodia and Syntyche who labored with Paul (Phil 4:2-3), and women who prayed and prophesied (1 Cor 11:5; Acts 21:9). The same letters contain the instructions on women's silence and teaching (1 Cor 14:34-35; 1 Tim 2:11-15). Whether those instructions are universal or tied to local circumstances is the core of the complementarian and egalitarian debate.

title: Widows and Orphans
summary: Without a husband or father to provide land, income and legal protection, widows and orphans were among the most vulnerable people in the ancient world. Scripture names them, with the sojourner, as the special concern of God and the test of a just society.
body:
In a society organized around the male head of household, losing him meant losing access to land, income and a voice at the city gate. A childless widow might return to her father's house, as Tamar was told to do (Gen 38:11), or face poverty, as Naomi did (Ruth 1:20-21). The Hebrew *almanah* (widow) and *yatom* (fatherless) are repeatedly paired with the *ger* (resident alien), the three groups with no natural protector.

Israel's law built protections around them. God executes justice for the fatherless and widow and loves the sojourner (Deut 10:18). They received the third-year tithe (Deut 14:28-29), the gleanings of field, olive tree and vineyard (Deut 24:19-22), and a widow's garment could not be taken in pledge (Deut 24:17). Mistreating them brings God's own wrath (Exod 22:22-24). Ruth's gleaning in Boaz's field shows these laws working (Ruth 2:2-17). God is called 'father of the fatherless and protector of widows' (Ps 68:5; Ps 146:9).

The prophets measured Judah's faithfulness by their treatment: 'defend the fatherless, plead for the widow' (Isa 1:17; Jer 22:3; Zech 7:10; Mal 3:5). Elijah is sent to a destitute widow of Zarephath and raises her son (1 Kgs 17:8-24), and Elisha multiplies a prophet's widow's oil to save her sons from debt slavery (2 Kgs 4:1-7).

In the gospels Jesus raises the only son of a widow at Nain, which restored her livelihood as much as her joy (Luke 7:11-17), condemns scribes who 'devour widows' houses' and praises the poor widow's two small coins (Mark 12:40-44). Anna, widowed for decades, is a prophetess in the temple (Luke 2:36-38). The early church organized daily food distribution for widows and chose seven men when Hellenist widows were neglected (Acts 6:1-6); Dorcas made clothing for widows at Joppa (Acts 9:36-41); 1 Timothy sets rules for an enrolled order of widows and insists families support their own (1 Tim 5:3-16). James defines pure religion as visiting orphans and widows in their affliction (Jas 1:27).

title: Covenant and Treaty Forms
summary: Israel's covenant with God, especially in Deuteronomy, closely follows the structure of ancient Near Eastern treaties between a great king and his vassals. The parallels illuminate what 'covenant' meant and feed a debate about when Deuteronomy took shape.
body:
Hittite kings of the fourteenth and thirteenth centuries BC bound subject rulers with written suzerainty treaties, such as Mursili II's treaty with Duppi-Teshub of Amurru. Their usual parts were: a preamble naming the great king; a historical prologue recounting his past kindness to the vassal; stipulations, beginning with exclusive loyalty; a clause for depositing the text in a temple and reading it publicly at intervals; a list of divine witnesses; and blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience. In the 1950s George Mendenhall drew attention to the parallels with Israel's covenant, and Meredith Kline developed them in *Treaty of the Great King* (1963).

The Sinai covenant opens in this way: 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt' is a preamble and a historical prologue in one sentence, followed by stipulations (Exod 20:2-17). Deuteronomy as a whole fits the pattern: preamble (Deut 1:1-5), historical prologue (Deut 1:6-4:49), general and specific stipulations (Deut 5-26), blessings and curses (Deut 27-28), deposit beside the ark and public reading every seven years (Deut 31:9-13; Deut 31:24-26), and witnesses, which in Israel's case are heaven and earth rather than gods (Deut 30:19; Deut 32:1). Joshua's covenant renewal at Shechem follows the same outline (Josh 24:1-27).

The dating question is real and debated. Scholars such as Kenneth Kitchen argue that the full Hittite form, with its historical prologue, belongs to the late second millennium, supporting an early origin for Deuteronomy's core. Others point to close parallels with the Neo-Assyrian Succession Treaty of Esarhaddon (672 BC), whose curses resemble Deuteronomy 28, for example a sky like bronze and earth like iron (Deut 28:23), and so connect the book with Josiah's reform in the seventh century (2 Kgs 22:8-23:3). Many see older material reshaped in later contexts.

Other covenant types also appear. Royal grant covenants, in which a king rewards a loyal servant unconditionally, resemble God's promises to Abraham and to David (Gen 15:7-21; 2 Sam 7:8-16). In Genesis 15 God alone passes between the halves of the animals, taking the self-curse on himself; Jeremiah shows the rite's meaning (Jer 34:18-20). The prophets accuse Israel of breaking covenant and announce a new covenant written on the heart (Jer 31:31-34), which Jesus invokes at the Last Supper and Hebrews expounds (Luke 22:20; Heb 8:6-13). How the covenants relate, and how conditional they are, shapes debates on Israel and the church and on salvation.

title: Purity and Food Laws
summary: The Torah divides the world into holy and common, clean and unclean, and regulates contact with impurity and the foods Israel may eat. These laws, including what later became 'kosher' practice, marked Israel off from the nations and were hotly debated in the early church.
body:
Ritual impurity in the Torah is a status, not in itself a sin. It came from natural sources: contact with a corpse (Num 19:11-16), certain skin diseases and mildews (Lev 13-14), genital discharges including menstruation and seminal emission (Lev 15), and childbirth (Lev 12). Most impurity was removed by waiting a set time, washing and, for the more serious kinds, offering a sacrifice; corpse impurity required water mixed with the ashes of a red heifer (Num 19:1-10). Impurity mattered chiefly because it must not come near the sanctuary, and the stated goal was holiness: 'you shall be holy, for I am holy' (Lev 11:44-45).

The food laws list which animals may be eaten (Lev 11; Deut 14:3-21). Land animals must both have a divided hoof and chew the cud, so the pig and camel are excluded; water creatures need fins and scales; certain birds, mostly predators and scavengers, are banned; among insects only kinds of locust are allowed (Lev 11:21-22). Blood must never be eaten, a rule given already to Noah (Gen 9:4; Lev 17:10-14), and a kid must not be boiled in its mother's milk (Exod 23:19; Deut 14:21), the root of later rabbinic separation of meat and dairy. Proposed rationales include hygiene, avoidance of pagan rites, and symbolic order, but the text itself grounds them in Israel's separation to God (Lev 20:24-26).

In the Second Temple period food and purity became identity markers. Daniel refuses the king's food (Dan 1:8), and Jews under Antiochus IV died rather than eat pork (1 Maccabees 1:62-63). Archaeology shows stepped immersion pools (*miqva'ot*) across Judea and Galilee and widespread stone vessels, which were thought not to contract impurity; John mentions six stone water jars 'for the Jewish rites of purification' at Cana (John 2:6). Pharisees sought to eat ordinary meals in a state of priestly purity and washed hands before eating (Mark 7:1-5).

Jesus touched lepers and a corpse and was touched by a woman with a flow of blood, reversing the direction of contagion (Mark 1:40-44; Mark 5:25-34; Luke 7:14). He taught that defilement comes from the heart, and Mark comments that he thereby declared all foods clean (Mark 7:14-23). Peter's vision and Cornelius' conversion apply this to table fellowship with Gentiles (Acts 10:9-16; Acts 10:28), the Jerusalem council asks Gentiles to avoid blood and strangled meat (Acts 15:19-20), and Paul argues that nothing is unclean in itself while urging care for weaker consciences (Rom 14:14-21; 1 Cor 8:1-13). The clash at Antioch over eating with Gentiles shows how hard this was in practice (Gal 2:11-14).

title: The Sacrificial System
summary: Leviticus sets out five main offerings plus daily, festival and Day of Atonement sacrifices, all centered on the altar of the tabernacle and later the temple. The New Testament interprets Jesus' death through this vocabulary.
body:
Leviticus 1-7 describes five main offerings. The burnt offering (*olah*) was wholly consumed on the altar and expressed total dedication and atonement (Lev 1). The grain offering (*minchah*) of flour, oil and frankincense was partly burned and partly eaten by priests (Lev 2). The peace or fellowship offering (*shelamim*) was shared: fat burned to God, portions to the priest, the rest eaten by the worshiper and family, often as thanksgiving or to fulfil a vow (Lev 3; Lev 7:11-18). The purification or sin offering (*chatta't*) cleansed the sanctuary and the offerer from unintentional sin and impurity, with the blood applied at different places according to the offerer's rank (Lev 4:1-5:13). The reparation or guilt offering (*asham*) dealt with sacrilege and wrongs that required restitution plus a fifth (Lev 5:14-6:7).

The offerer typically laid a hand on the animal's head, which many read as identification or transfer (Lev 1:4), and the blood was central because 'the life of the flesh is in the blood' and God gave it on the altar to make atonement (Lev 17:11). The poor could bring two birds or flour instead of a lamb (Lev 5:7-11), which is what Mary and Joseph offered at Jesus' presentation (Luke 2:22-24). Twice daily a lamb was offered as the continual (*tamid*) offering (Exod 29:38-42; Num 28:3-8), and festivals added more (Num 28-29).

On the Day of Atonement the high priest entered the most holy place with blood to purge the sanctuary, and a second goat bearing the people's sins was sent into the wilderness (Lev 16). Unlike many neighboring cults, Israel's sacrifices were not food for a hungry god; Psalm 50 mocks the idea (Ps 50:12-13). The prophets insisted that sacrifice without justice and mercy was worthless (Isa 1:11-17; Hos 6:6; Mic 6:6-8; Ps 51:16-17), a theme Jesus quotes (Matt 9:13).

The New Testament describes Jesus as the Lamb of God (John 1:29), the Passover lamb (1 Cor 5:7), a ransom (Mark 10:45) and a sacrifice whose blood establishes the covenant (Mark 14:24). Hebrews argues at length that his single offering fulfils and ends the repeated sacrifices (Heb 9:11-14; Heb 10:1-18). Sacrifice at the Jerusalem temple ceased when the Romans destroyed it in AD 70. How exactly Jesus' death relates to these categories, whether as penal substitution, purification, victory, or example, is the subject of the atonement debate.

title: Sabbath, Sabbatical Year and Jubilee
summary: Israel's calendar was built on sevens: a weekly day of rest, a seventh year of fallow land and debt release, and a fiftieth year when land returned to its families. Sabbath became a defining mark of Jewish identity and a frequent flashpoint in Jesus' ministry.
body:
The Sabbath is rooted in creation, when God rested on the seventh day and blessed it (Gen 2:2-3). The Exodus form of the commandment grounds it in that rest (Exod 20:8-11), while Deuteronomy grounds it in the release from slavery and extends rest explicitly to servants and animals (Deut 5:12-15). It was a covenant sign between God and Israel (Exod 31:12-17), first practised with the manna (Exod 16:22-30). Prophets and reformers treated it as a test of loyalty: Jeremiah warned against carrying loads through Jerusalem's gates (Jer 17:21-27) and Nehemiah shut the gates against Sabbath traders (Neh 13:15-22).

Every seventh year the land lay fallow and its spontaneous growth belonged to the poor and wild animals (Exod 23:10-11; Lev 25:1-7), and debts between Israelites were released (Deut 15:1-11). After seven sabbatical cycles came the jubilee, announced by the ram's horn on the Day of Atonement: land returned to its original families and Israelite debt-servants went free (Lev 25:8-55). Whether the jubilee was ever fully practised is debated; the Chronicler interprets the seventy years of exile as the land enjoying its neglected sabbaths (2 Chr 36:21).

In the Second Temple period Sabbath keeping was detailed and serious. Early in the Maccabean revolt pious Jews let themselves be killed rather than fight on the Sabbath, after which Mattathias ruled that defensive fighting was permitted (1 Maccabees 2:29-41). The Mishnah later lists thirty-nine main categories of forbidden work (Shabbat 7:2). A 'Sabbath day's journey' was about 2,000 cubits, roughly a kilometer (Acts 1:12). Hillel is credited with the *prozbul*, a legal device that let creditors collect debts despite the sabbatical year, because lenders were refusing loans.

Jesus regularly taught in synagogues on the Sabbath (Luke 4:16), but his healings and his disciples' plucking of grain provoked disputes. He argued from David, from the priests' temple work and from the Sabbath's purpose: 'the Sabbath was made for man' and the Son of Man is lord of it (Mark 2:23-3:6; John 5:1-18). At Nazareth he read the jubilee-shaped promise of Isaiah 61, 'the year of the Lord's favor', and declared it fulfilled (Isa 61:1-2; Luke 4:16-21). Paul treats special days as a matter of conscience and calls Sabbaths a shadow of Christ (Rom 14:5-6; Col 2:16-17), Hebrews speaks of a Sabbath rest remaining for God's people (Heb 4:1-11), and the church gathered on the first day of the week (Acts 20:7; 1 Cor 16:2; Rev 1:10). Christians still differ on whether the Sabbath command carries over to Sunday.

title: The Tabernacle
summary: The tabernacle was the portable tent-sanctuary Israel built at Sinai so that God could dwell among them on the journey. Its layout, furnishings and graded holiness shaped the later temple and much New Testament imagery.
body:
Exodus devotes thirteen chapters to the tabernacle, giving the instructions (Exod 25-31) and then describing their execution almost word for word (Exod 35-40), which signals its importance. Its purpose is stated at the start: 'let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst' (Exod 25:8). The craftsman Bezalel of Judah and his assistant Oholiab of Dan are said to be filled with the Spirit of God for skilled work (Exod 31:1-6), and the people's gifts were so generous that Moses had to tell them to stop (Exod 36:5-7).

The courtyard measured 100 by 50 cubits, roughly 45 by 23 meters, enclosed by linen hangings (Exod 27:9-18). Inside stood the bronze altar of burnt offering, 5 cubits square and 3 high (Exod 27:1), and the bronze basin for priestly washing (Exod 30:17-21). The tent itself, about 30 by 10 cubits on the usual reconstruction, had two rooms. The holy place held the table for the bread of the presence, the seven-branched golden lampstand and the incense altar (Exod 25:23-40; Exod 30:1-10). Behind the veil the most holy place, a perfect cube of 10 cubits, held the ark of the covenant: an acacia chest 2.5 by 1.5 by 1.5 cubits overlaid with gold, containing the tablets, with a gold cover (*kapporet*, the 'mercy seat' or 'atonement cover') flanked by two cherubim (Exod 25:10-22).

Holiness increased from the camp to the courtyard to the holy place to the most holy place, and access narrowed accordingly: Israelites to the courtyard, priests to the holy place, the high priest alone into the inner room once a year (Lev 16:2; Heb 9:6-7). The tribes camped around it in a fixed order with the Levites nearest (Num 2-3). When it was completed, the cloud covered the tent and the glory of the LORD filled it (Exod 40:34-38). Scholars have noted parallels with Egyptian portable shrines and with the layout of Ramesses II's royal war camp, and also echoes of Eden: cherubim, gold, precious stones and an eastward entrance.

After the conquest the tabernacle stood at Shiloh, where Eli and the young Samuel served (Josh 18:1; 1 Sam 1:3; 1 Sam 3:3), until the temple replaced it. The New Testament draws on it repeatedly: the Word 'tabernacled' among us and we saw his glory (John 1:14), the earthly tent was a copy and shadow of the heavenly one (Heb 8:5; Heb 9:1-12), and the final vision announces that the dwelling of God is with humanity (Rev 21:3). Christians have long read its details typologically, though how far to press them is debated.

title: The Temple, Its Priests and Its Music
summary: Jerusalem's temple, built by Solomon, rebuilt after the exile and vastly expanded by Herod, was the center of Israel's sacrifice, pilgrimage, economy and song. Its priestly courses and Levitical musicians gave Israel the setting in which the Psalms were sung.
body:
Solomon's temple, built in seven years, was 60 cubits long, 20 wide and 30 high, a long-room plan with porch, main hall and inner sanctuary, similar to Syrian temples such as the one excavated at Ain Dara (1 Kgs 6:2; 1 Kgs 6:37-38). At its dedication the glory cloud filled the house (1 Kgs 8:10-11). The Babylonians burned it in 586 BC (2 Kgs 25:8-17). Returning exiles under Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest completed a modest second temple in 515 BC, encouraged by Haggai and Zechariah (Ezra 6:14-15; Hag 2:3). Herod the Great began rebuilding it around 20/19 BC; the work was still going on when Jesus' opponents said it had taken forty-six years (John 2:20), and it was finished only a few years before the Romans destroyed it in AD 70.

Herod doubled the Temple Mount platform to about 144,000 square meters, roughly 35 acres, supported by massive retaining walls whose lower courses survive as the Western Wall. Outer porticoes, including Solomon's Portico where Jesus and the apostles taught (John 10:23; Acts 3:11), surrounded the Court of the Gentiles. A low barrier carried Greek inscriptions, two of which have been found, warning foreigners not to enter further on pain of death; Paul was accused of bringing a Gentile past it (Acts 21:27-29). Within lay the Court of Women, the Court of Israel, the Court of the Priests with the altar, and the sanctuary with its veil (Mark 15:38).

The priests were divided into twenty-four courses that served a week at a time, twice a year, plus at festivals (1 Chr 24:1-19). Zechariah belonged to the course of Abijah and was chosen by lot to burn incense (Luke 1:5-9). Chief priests from a few aristocratic families controlled the institution; Annas and five of his sons, and his son-in-law Caiaphas, held the high priesthood. The temple was also a treasury and economic hub: every adult Jewish male paid a half-shekel tax (Exod 30:13; Matt 17:24-27), money changers converted coins into the high-silver Tyrian shekel, and animals were sold for sacrifice, which is the setting of Jesus' action in the courts (Mark 11:15-17).

Music accompanied worship. Chronicles assigns Levitical guilds led by Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun to prophesy with lyres, harps and cymbals (1 Chr 25:1-7), and priests sounded silver trumpets (Num 10:1-10; 2 Chr 5:12-13). The Psalter, 150 psalms in five books each ending with a doxology (Ps 41:13; Ps 72:19; Ps 89:52; Ps 106:48), gathers prayers and songs from David to the post-exilic period. Superscriptions name a psalm 'for the Sabbath' (Ps 92), the Songs of Ascents were sung by pilgrims (Ps 120-134), and the Hallel (Ps 113-118) was sung at Passover; the hymn Jesus and his disciples sang after the Supper was probably part of it (Mark 14:26). The church carried the habit forward in psalms, hymns and spiritual songs (Col 3:16; Eph 5:19).

title: The Synagogue
summary: The synagogue was the local Jewish assembly and its building, where scripture was read and taught on the Sabbath. It was the main venue of Jesus' Galilean teaching and Paul's first stop in each city.
body:
The word *synagoge* means 'gathering' and could refer to a congregation or its building; Jews in the diaspora often used *proseuche*, 'place of prayer' (Acts 16:13). Its origins are debated. Many have traced it to the Babylonian exile, when the temple was out of reach, but the earliest firm evidence is inscriptions from Ptolemaic Egypt in the third century BC dedicating prayer houses. In the land of Israel, pre-70 synagogue buildings have been excavated at Gamla, Masada, Herodium, Magdala and elsewhere. The Theodotus inscription from Jerusalem, usually dated before AD 70, says a priest and synagogue leader built it 'for the reading of the law and the teaching of the commandments' with lodging for visitors from abroad.

A typical early synagogue was a rectangular hall with stepped stone benches along the walls facing the center, so that the congregation faced one another and the reader. At Magdala, excavated from 2009, a carved stone block bearing a menorah may have served as a reading table. The famous white limestone synagogue at Capernaum dates to the fourth or fifth century, but beneath it lies a basalt floor that may belong to the first-century building Jesus taught in (Mark 1:21). Jesus refers to the 'seat of Moses' (Matt 23:2), and later stone chairs found at Chorazin and elsewhere may illustrate the phrase.

The Sabbath service included the Shema (Deut 6:4-9), prayers, a reading from the Torah and one from the Prophets, and a sermon or exposition. Luke gives the earliest detailed description: Jesus stands to read from the Isaiah scroll handed to him by the attendant, then sits to teach (Luke 4:16-21). At Pisidian Antioch the rulers invite Paul and Barnabas to give a 'word of exhortation' after the readings (Acts 13:14-15), and James notes that Moses is read in every city's synagogues every Sabbath (Acts 15:21). Officials included the ruler of the synagogue, such as Jairus or Crispus (Luke 8:41; Acts 18:8), and the attendant (Luke 4:20). Synagogues also judged local cases and administered discipline, including flogging (Matt 10:17; 2 Cor 11:24).

Paul's custom was to go first to the synagogue (Acts 17:1-3), where he found not only Jews but Gentile 'God-fearers' attached to Judaism (Acts 13:16; Acts 13:26), and many of his first converts came from this group. John's gospel speaks of believers being put out of the synagogue (John 9:22; John 16:2); how and when a formal separation happened is debated. The synagogue's pattern of reading, exposition, prayer and alms shaped early Christian worship.

title: Festivals and the Jewish Calendar
summary: Israel's year ran on a lunar calendar adjusted to the agricultural seasons, with three pilgrimage festivals and several holy days. Much of the gospel and Acts narrative is timed by these feasts.
body:
Months began with the new moon, giving a year of about 354 days; to keep festivals tied to the harvests an extra month (a second Adar) was added roughly seven times in nineteen years. Pre-exilic texts use Canaanite month names such as Abib, Ziv, Ethanim and Bul (Exod 13:4; 1 Kgs 6:1; 1 Kgs 6:38; 1 Kgs 8:2), while post-exilic books use Babylonian names: Nisan, Iyyar, Sivan, Tammuz, Av, Elul, Tishri, Marcheshvan, Kislev, Tevet, Shevat and Adar (Neh 2:1; Esth 3:7). The religious year began in spring with Nisan (Exod 12:2), while the civil and agricultural year turned in autumn. The Qumran community and the book of Jubilees championed a rival 364-day solar calendar, so not all Jews kept feasts on the same days.

The Torah required men to appear before the LORD three times a year (Exod 23:14-17; Deut 16:16). Passover on 14 Nisan, followed by the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread, recalled the exodus and coincided with the barley harvest (Exod 12:1-20; Lev 23:4-14). The Feast of Weeks, fifty days later and so called Pentecost in Greek, celebrated the wheat harvest (Lev 23:15-21; Acts 2:1). The Feast of Booths or Tabernacles, from 15 Tishri, marked the fruit and olive ingathering, with families living in shelters to recall the wilderness (Lev 23:33-43). In the first century water was drawn from Siloam and poured at the altar and great lamps lit the temple courts, the background to Jesus' words about living water and the light of the world (John 7:37-38; John 8:12).

Autumn also brought the day of trumpets on 1 Tishri (Lev 23:23-25), later Rosh Hashanah, and the Day of Atonement on 10 Tishri, a fast day of national cleansing (Lev 16:29-34; Lev 23:26-32); Luke dates a dangerous voyage by it, calling it 'the Fast' (Acts 27:9). Later feasts were Purim in Adar, commemorating deliverance in Esther's day (Esth 9:20-32), and Hanukkah or Dedication in Kislev, commemorating the Maccabean rededication of the temple, at which Jesus was in Jerusalem (John 10:22-23).

Pilgrim crowds swelled Jerusalem at Passover. Josephus gives figures in the millions that are generally thought inflated; modern estimates range from around a hundred thousand to several hundred thousand. John's gospel structures Jesus' ministry around at least three Passovers (John 2:13; John 6:4; John 11:55). Whether the Last Supper was itself a Passover meal, as the Synoptics present it (Mark 14:12-16), or held the evening before, with Jesus dying as the lambs were slaughtered, as John's timing may suggest (John 18:28; John 19:14), is an old and unresolved question.

title: Assyrian Deportation Policy
summary: From Tiglath-pileser III onward, Assyria systematically moved conquered populations across its empire to break resistance and supply labor. This policy ended the northern kingdom of Israel and created the mixed population of Samaria.
body:
Mass deportation was an Assyrian imperial tool before the eighth century, but Tiglath-pileser III (745-727 BC) made it routine and two-directional: rebels were removed from their homeland and replaced by peoples from elsewhere. The aims were practical: to break local loyalties, punish revolt, populate new cities and farmland, and supply soldiers and workers. Assyriologist Bustenay Oded estimated that some four and a half million people were moved over about three centuries, though such totals are necessarily rough. Assyrian reliefs show deportees walking with their families and belongings, not chained in long lines, because they were valuable as settlers.

Israel felt this in stages. Tiglath-pileser took Galilee, Gilead and the territory of Naphtali in 733/732 BC and carried the people to Assyria (2 Kgs 15:29). After a three-year siege Samaria fell in 722/721 BC; Shalmaneser V began the siege and Sargon II claims the conquest, recording in his inscriptions that he deported 27,290 people (other copies give 27,280). The biblical account places the exiles in Halah, on the Habor river of Gozan and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kgs 17:5-6), and says the king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim to resettle Samaria (2 Kgs 17:24). The narrator explains the disaster theologically as the result of covenant unfaithfulness (2 Kgs 17:7-23), as Hosea and Amos had warned (Hos 9:3; Amos 7:17).

Judah nearly suffered the same fate. In 701 BC Sennacherib took Lachish and many towns; his prism claims he took 200,150 people from Judah, a figure many think inflated, and his Nineveh palace reliefs show Lachish's families being led away. His envoy offered Jerusalem's defenders peaceful deportation 'to a land like your own land' (2 Kgs 18:31-32), but the city was spared (2 Kgs 19:32-36; Isa 37:33-37).

The resettlement of Samaria lies behind later Jewish-Samaritan hostility, since Judeans described the Samaritans as descendants of these colonists (2 Kgs 17:24-41). The idea of 'ten lost tribes' is too simple: many northerners stayed or fled south, Hezekiah invited survivors to Passover (2 Chr 30:1-11), and Luke introduces Anna as from the tribe of Asher (Luke 2:36). Assyria's brutality explains why Jonah resisted preaching to Nineveh and why Nahum celebrates its fall in 612 BC (Jonah 4:1-2; Nah 3:1-7).

title: Life in the Babylonian Exile
summary: Judeans were taken to Babylonia in several waves between 605 and 582 BC, where they mostly lived in their own communities as farmers and workers. Exile reshaped Judaism around scripture, Sabbath and identity without a temple.
body:
Babylon took captives from Judah in stages. Daniel and other young nobles were taken around 605 BC (Dan 1:1-6). In 597 BC Nebuchadnezzar deported King Jehoiachin, his court, warriors and craftsmen, about ten thousand people including Ezekiel (2 Kgs 24:10-16). After the rebellion of Zedekiah, Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed in 586 BC and more were taken (2 Kgs 25:8-12), and a further deportation followed in 582 BC; Jeremiah gives totals of 3,023, 832 and 745, 4,600 in all, probably counting adult men (Jer 52:28-30). The poorest were left to work the land (2 Kgs 25:12).

Unlike the Assyrians, the Babylonians did not usually import foreigners into conquered land, and they settled deportees in groups. Ezekiel lived among exiles at Tel-abib by the Chebar canal near Nippur (Ezek 1:1-3; Ezek 3:15), and elders could gather in his house (Ezek 8:1). Cuneiform tablets from a town called Al-Yahudu, 'Judah-town', dating from about 572 to 477 BC, show Judeans farming land held from the crown, paying taxes, making contracts and giving children names built on the divine name Yahweh. Ration tablets found in Babylon list oil for 'Ya'u-kinu, king of the land of Yahud', confirming Jehoiachin's presence at court and his later release (2 Kgs 25:27-30).

Jeremiah's letter told the exiles to build houses, plant gardens, marry and seek the welfare of the city, because the exile would last seventy years (Jer 29:4-10). Some rose high in the administration, as Daniel and his friends did, receiving Babylonian names and education while trying to keep their distinct practices (Dan 1:4-8). Others mourned bitterly by the rivers of Babylon (Ps 137:1-6).

Without the temple, identity centered on what could be carried: circumcision, Sabbath, food laws, prayer toward Jerusalem (Dan 6:10), and above all the scriptures, which many scholars think were collected and edited in this period. Prophets such as Ezekiel and the later chapters of Isaiah reinterpreted the catastrophe as judgment and promised a new exodus (Ezek 36:24-28; Isa 40:1-5). When Cyrus allowed return, many stayed; Babylonian Jewry remained a major center for more than a thousand years and later produced the Babylonian Talmud.

title: Persian Policy and the Cyrus Cylinder
summary: Cyrus the Great took Babylon in 539 BC and, like later Persian kings, allowed deported peoples and their gods to return home. The Cyrus Cylinder records this policy, and Ezra-Nehemiah describe its effect on Judah.
body:
Cyrus II of Persia captured Babylon in October 539 BC, largely without a battle. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay barrel inscribed in Akkadian and discovered at Babylon in 1879, presents him as chosen by Babylon's god Marduk to replace the impious Nabonidus. It says he returned the images of gods to their sanctuaries in cities across the Tigris and gathered their former inhabitants back to their homes. The cylinder does not mention Judah, and the policy was conventional royal propaganda as well as pragmatic statecraft: restored local cults prayed for the king and kept provinces content. Even so, it matches the biblical picture well.

The Bible records Cyrus' decree in Hebrew (Ezra 1:1-4; 2 Chr 36:22-23) and in an Aramaic memorandum found later in the archive at Ecbatana, which specifies the temple's dimensions and that costs be paid from the royal treasury (Ezra 6:1-5). Isaiah names Cyrus as the LORD's shepherd and anointed (Isa 44:28-45:1); traditional scholars see predictive prophecy, while many critical scholars date these chapters to the exile itself, a question bound up with views of inspiration. The returning exiles, led by Sheshbazzar and then Zerubbabel and Joshua, numbered 42,360 plus servants (Ezra 2:64-65).

The Persian empire was organized into satrapies with Imperial Aramaic as the administrative language, which is why parts of Ezra are in Aramaic (Ezra 4:8-6:18; Ezra 7:12-26). Opposition from neighbors delayed the temple until Darius I confirmed Cyrus' decree; it was finished in 515 BC (Ezra 6:6-15). Artaxerxes I sent Ezra the scribe with authority to teach and enforce the law of God (Ezra 7:11-26) and later appointed his cupbearer Nehemiah governor to rebuild Jerusalem's walls (Neh 2:1-8). A royal courier system carried edicts quickly across the empire, as Esther describes (Esth 3:13-15; Esth 8:10).

Papyri from Elephantine, a Jewish military colony on the Nile, illuminate the period: a letter of 407 BC asks Bagohi, governor of Judah, for permission to rebuild their destroyed temple of Yahu, and mentions Sanballat's sons in Samaria (compare Neh 2:19). Persian rule over Judea lasted about two centuries, until Alexander's conquest in 332 BC, and Daniel and Esther both portray Jews serving at the Persian court (Dan 6:1-3; Esth 2:5-8).

title: Hellenization
summary: After Alexander the Great's conquests, Greek language, cities and culture spread across the Near East, including Judea. Jews adopted, adapted and resisted Hellenism in varying degrees, and the New Testament itself was written in Greek.
body:
Alexander of Macedon defeated Persia at Issus in 333 BC, besieged Tyre and Gaza in 332, and took control of Judea on the way to Egypt. After his death in 323 BC his generals divided the empire. Judea was ruled by the Ptolemies of Egypt until about 200 BC, when the Seleucids of Syria won it at the battle of Panium. Daniel's visions of the goat with a great horn broken into four and of the kings of the north and south are commonly read against this history (Dan 8:5-8; Dan 8:21-22; Dan 11:2-4).

Hellenization meant Greek as the common language of trade and government (*koine*, 'common' Greek), Greek-style cities with gymnasium, theater and council, and Greek education, philosophy and religion. In Alexandria, Jews translated their scriptures into Greek from the third century BC; the legend in the *Letter of Aristeas* attributes the Torah's translation to seventy-two elders, hence the name Septuagint. In Jerusalem the high priest Jason built a gymnasium around 175 BC, and some young men tried to hide their circumcision (1 Maccabees 1:14-15; 2 Maccabees 4:9-15), provoking deep division.

By the first century Greek cities ringed Galilee: the Decapolis east of the Jordan (Mark 5:20; Mark 7:31), coastal cities such as Caesarea, and Herodian foundations such as Sepphoris and Tiberias (John 6:23). Martin Hengel showed that Palestinian Judaism was itself thoroughly touched by Hellenism, so a sharp line between 'Palestinian' and 'Hellenistic' Judaism is misleading. Many Galileans were probably bilingual in Aramaic and some Greek, and Greek inscriptions and names are common even in Jerusalem.

The church was born into this world. Acts distinguishes Hebrew-speaking and Greek-speaking Jewish believers (Acts 6:1), and the seven chosen to serve all have Greek names (Acts 6:5). Greeks seek Jesus at the feast (John 12:20-21), Paul debates philosophers in Athens (Acts 17:16-34), and every New Testament book was written in Greek, usually quoting the Septuagint. How much Greek thought shaped early theology, for example John's use of *logos* (John 1:1), is debated.

title: The Maccabees and Hanukkah
summary: When Antiochus IV outlawed Judaism and defiled the temple in 167 BC, a priestly family led a revolt that rededicated the temple in 164 BC and founded the Hasmonean dynasty. Hanukkah commemorates the rededication.
body:
Antiochus IV Epiphanes, Seleucid king from 175 BC, intervened repeatedly in Jerusalem's high-priestly politics and plundered the temple. Around 167 BC, after unrest in Jerusalem, he issued decrees banning circumcision, Sabbath observance and the Torah, and on 15 Kislev an altar to Olympian Zeus was set up on the altar of burnt offering, the 'abomination of desolation' (1 Maccabees 1:41-64). Daniel's visions describe a king who profanes the sanctuary, removes the regular burnt offering and sets up 'the abomination that makes desolate' (Dan 11:31; Dan 12:11), and Jesus later uses the phrase for a coming desecration (Matt 24:15; Mark 13:14).

At Modein the aged priest Mattathias killed a Jew offering pagan sacrifice and the king's officer, and fled to the hills with his five sons (1 Maccabees 2:15-28). His son Judas, nicknamed Maccabeus, 'the hammer', led guerrilla victories against larger Seleucid armies. On 25 Kislev 164 BC Judas' forces cleansed the temple, built a new altar and celebrated an eight-day dedication, decreeing that it be kept yearly (1 Maccabees 4:52-59). John's gospel places Jesus in the temple at this 'Feast of Dedication' in winter (John 10:22-23). The story of a single cruse of oil lasting eight days appears much later, in the Babylonian Talmud.

The revolt became a dynasty. Judas' brother Jonathan became high priest in 152 BC, and Simon won effective independence in 142 BC. John Hyrcanus conquered Idumea and forced its people to be circumcised, and destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim. Alexander Jannaeus, king and high priest, was hated by the Pharisees and, according to Josephus, crucified eight hundred opponents (*Antiquities* 13.380). Civil war between his sons gave the Roman general Pompey the opportunity to take Jerusalem in 63 BC.

The Maccabean era shaped the world of the New Testament: it produced the parties of Pharisees and Sadducees, a tradition of zeal for the law, martyr stories that strengthened belief in bodily resurrection (2 Maccabees 7), and hopes for a liberator. Hebrews' list of those who were tortured, refusing release, to rise to a better life probably alludes to these martyrs (Heb 11:35-38). The books of Maccabees are in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles but in the Protestant Apocrypha.

title: Roman Occupation of Judea
summary: Rome controlled Judea from 63 BC, first through client kings and from AD 6 through governors such as Pontius Pilate. Roman power framed Jesus' trial, Paul's imprisonments and the catastrophe of AD 70.
body:
Pompey entered Jerusalem in 63 BC and made Judea tributary. Rome then ruled through Hasmonean figures and, from 40/37 BC, through Herod the Great as client king. When Herod's son Archelaus proved incompetent, Augustus deposed him in AD 6 and placed Judea, with Samaria and Idumea, under an equestrian governor based at Caesarea Maritima, subordinate to the legate of Syria. Galilee remained under Herod Antipas, so Jesus grew up under a Jewish client ruler, while Jerusalem was under direct Roman rule. Luke dates events by the reigns of Augustus and Tiberius and the governorships of Quirinius and Pilate (Luke 2:1-2; Luke 3:1).

Pontius Pilate governed from AD 26 to 36; a stone found at Caesarea in 1961 names him 'prefect of Judea'. Governors commanded auxiliary troops, around three thousand, mostly recruited locally from non-Jewish cities, and moved to Jerusalem at festivals, garrisoning the Antonia fortress beside the temple, from which the tribune Claudius Lysias rescued Paul (Acts 21:31-36). Centurions appear often and sometimes sympathetically (Matt 8:5-13; Mark 15:39; Acts 10:1-2). Soldiers could compel civilians to carry loads, the background of 'going the second mile' and of Simon of Cyrene carrying the cross (Matt 5:41; Mark 15:21).

Rome usually left local matters to the high priest and council, but kept capital jurisdiction, as John notes (John 18:31). Jews were exempted from military service and from emperor sacrifice, offering sacrifices on the emperor's behalf instead. Tensions flared over taxes, images and money: Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the census of AD 6 (Acts 5:37), Pilate provoked crowds with military standards and by taking temple funds for an aqueduct, and Luke mentions Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled with their sacrifices (Luke 13:1). The question 'Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar?' was a trap precisely because of this (Mark 12:13-17).

After AD 44 governors such as Felix and Festus, before whom Paul appeared (Acts 24:1-27; Acts 25:1-12), presided over growing unrest. In AD 66 revolt broke out; Titus captured Jerusalem and burned the temple in August AD 70, and Masada fell in 73 or 74. Jesus' warnings about the temple's destruction (Mark 13:1-2; Luke 19:41-44; Luke 21:20-24) are read by some as fulfilled entirely in AD 70 and by others as foreshadowing a final end, a key question in eschatology. Paul's instruction to submit to governing authorities (Rom 13:1-7) and Revelation's portrait of Rome as a beast (Rev 13:1-8) show two sides of early Christian response.

title: The Herodian Dynasty
summary: Herod the Great and his descendants ruled parts of the Jewish homeland as Roman clients from 37 BC to the end of the first century. Five different Herods appear in the New Testament, and keeping them apart clarifies many passages.
body:
Herod the Great was the son of Antipater, an Idumean whose family had been converted under the Hasmoneans. Rome's Senate named him king of Judea in 40 BC, and he took Jerusalem in 37 BC. He was a gifted administrator and one of antiquity's great builders: he rebuilt the temple on a vast platform, created the artificial harbor city of Caesarea Maritima, and built palace-fortresses at Masada, Machaerus and the Herodium, where archaeologist Ehud Netzer identified his tomb in 2007. He was also paranoid and brutal, executing his wife Mariamne and three of his sons. Matthew's account of the massacre of Bethlehem's infants (Matt 2:1-18) is not attested elsewhere but fits his character. He died in 4 BC on the usual reckoning, which is why Jesus' birth is dated before then; a minority argue for 1 BC.

Herod's will divided his realm among three sons, confirmed by Augustus. Archelaus received Judea, Samaria and Idumea as ethnarch, and his reputation is why Joseph settled in Galilee rather than Judea (Matt 2:22-23); he was deposed in AD 6. Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea as tetrarch until AD 39, built Tiberias, married his half-brother's wife Herodias, imprisoned and beheaded John the Baptist (Mark 6:14-29), was called 'that fox' by Jesus (Luke 13:31-32) and questioned Jesus during his trial (Luke 23:6-12). Philip ruled the north-east, refounding Paneas as Caesarea Philippi and Bethsaida as Julias (Luke 3:1; Mark 8:27).

Herod Agrippa I, a grandson of Herod the Great raised in Rome, became king over nearly all his grandfather's territory by AD 41. He executed James the son of Zebedee and imprisoned Peter, and died suddenly at Caesarea in AD 44 after accepting divine acclaim (Acts 12:1-23); Josephus describes the same death (*Antiquities* 19.343-350). His son Agrippa II, with his sister Bernice, heard Paul's defense before Festus and remarked that Paul would soon persuade him to be a Christian (Acts 25:13-26:32). Agrippa I's daughter Drusilla was the wife of the governor Felix (Acts 24:24).

The 'Herodians' who joined Pharisees against Jesus were probably supporters of the dynasty (Mark 3:6; Mark 12:13). For many Jews the Herods were compromised: Idumean in origin, Roman in loyalty and Hellenistic in style, yet patrons of the temple. Their story frames the New Testament from Jesus' birth to Paul's last hearing in Judea.

title: Taxation and Tax Collectors
summary: First-century Jews owed Roman tribute, tolls and customs, Herodian taxes, and religious dues such as tithes and the temple tax. Toll collectors, who worked for these systems and often profited from them, were widely despised.
body:
Roman taxation had two main forms. Direct taxes were a land tax (*tributum soli*), often paid in produce, and a poll tax (*tributum capitis*) on persons; in Judea after AD 6 these were assessed by census, which is why the census of Quirinius provoked revolt (Acts 5:37). The tribute was paid in Roman coin, and the denarius bearing Caesar's image and inscription is the coin Jesus asks to see (Mark 12:13-17). Indirect taxes included tolls on roads, bridges and ports, market dues and customs on goods in transit. These were commonly farmed out: contractors bid for the right to collect a district's dues, paid the authorities in advance and recovered their outlay with a profit.

The *telonai* of the gospels, traditionally 'publicans', were mostly local toll collectors, often Jews, working for these contractors or for Herod Antipas in Galilee. Levi, also called Matthew, sat at a toll office in Capernaum, a border town on a trade route between Antipas' and Philip's territories (Mark 2:14; Matt 9:9). Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector at Jericho, a major customs point on the route from Perea, and was rich (Luke 19:1-2). Collectors could overcharge, which is why John the Baptist tells them to collect no more than is appointed (Luke 3:12-13), and Zacchaeus' promise to repay fourfold matches the Torah's penalty for theft of a sheep (Luke 19:8; Exod 22:1).

Religious dues added to the load. Israelites owed tithes of produce for Levites and priests, a second tithe to be eaten in Jerusalem, and a third-year tithe for the poor, though how these combined in practice is debated (Num 18:21-24; Deut 14:22-29). Pharisees tithed even garden herbs (Matt 23:23). Every adult male paid the half-shekel temple tax (Matt 17:24-27). Scholars' estimates of the total burden on a Galilean farmer vary widely, but it was heavy, and debt and loss of land were common themes in Jesus' parables (Matt 18:23-34; Luke 16:1-8).

Tax collectors were grouped with sinners and prostitutes (Matt 9:10-11; Matt 21:31-32) because of their dishonesty, their constant contact with Gentiles and their collaboration with occupying power. Jesus' choice of Matthew as a disciple, his meals with tax collectors, and the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector (Luke 18:9-14) were therefore provocative. Paul nonetheless tells believers to pay taxes and tolls to whom they are owed (Rom 13:6-7).

title: Crucifixion
summary: Crucifixion was a Roman method of execution designed to be slow, public and humiliating, used mainly for slaves, rebels and non-citizens. Its horror and shame are the background to the New Testament's message of a crucified Messiah.
body:
Forms of impaling or hanging bodies on stakes were used by Assyrians, Persians and Carthaginians, and Alexander crucified defenders of Tyre. Rome made crucifixion its standard 'slaves' punishment' and the penalty for rebellion and banditry in the provinces. Roman citizens were normally exempt; Cicero calls it the cruelest and most disgusting penalty (*Against Verres* 2.5.165). Mass crucifixions served as warnings: Josephus says the Syrian legate Varus crucified two thousand rebels around Jerusalem in 4 BC (*Antiquities* 17.295), and during the siege of AD 70 Titus crucified so many that wood ran short (*Jewish War* 5.451). Earlier the Hasmonean Alexander Jannaeus had crucified eight hundred Jewish opponents.

The procedure varied but often included flogging with a whip of leather thongs weighted with bone or metal (Mark 15:15), mockery (Mark 15:16-20), and the condemned carrying the crossbeam (*patibulum*) to the site (John 19:17). A placard (*titulus*) stated the charge; Jesus' read 'King of the Jews' in Hebrew, Latin and Greek (John 19:19-20). Victims were tied or nailed; the heel bone of a man named Jehohanan, found in a Jerusalem ossuary in 1968, still has an iron nail about 11.5 cm long driven through it from the side. Crucifixions took place beside roads so that passers-by would see (Mark 15:29). Victims were stripped, and executioners took their clothes (John 19:23-24).

Death came from exhaustion, shock, blood loss and difficulty breathing, and could take hours or days; Pilate was surprised that Jesus died within about six hours (Mark 15:44). Breaking the legs (*crurifragium*) hastened death, and John says the soldiers did this to the two men crucified with Jesus because the Sabbath was coming (John 19:31-33). Romans often left bodies to rot, but Jewish law required burial before nightfall (Deut 21:22-23), which explains Joseph of Arimathea's request (Mark 15:42-46).

Because Deuteronomy pronounced anyone hanged on a tree to be under God's curse, a crucified Messiah was a scandal to Jews and folly to Gentiles (1 Cor 1:23). Paul argues that Christ became a curse for us (Gal 3:13), and Hebrews says he endured the cross, despising its shame (Heb 12:2). A graffito from the Palatine in Rome, usually dated to the second or third century, mocks a Christian named Alexamenos for worshipping a crucified figure with a donkey's head. The early Christians' willingness to proclaim the cross, rather than hide it, is itself historically striking.

title: The Pharisees
summary: The Pharisees were a popular lay movement devoted to precise observance of the Torah as interpreted by the 'tradition of the elders'. They were Jesus' most frequent conversation partners and critics, Paul's former party, and the forerunners of rabbinic Judaism.
body:
The name probably comes from Hebrew *perushim*, 'separated ones'. The movement emerges in the Hasmonean period of the second century BC, at times influential at court and at times persecuted. Josephus, who claimed to follow their way, says there were more than six thousand in Herod's time (*Antiquities* 17.42) and that they had great influence with the common people. Most were not priests but laymen, many of them artisans and merchants, organized in fellowships committed to tithing and purity.

Their distinctives, according to Josephus and the New Testament, were: the binding authority of ancestral traditions not written in the law of Moses (Mark 7:3-5), later called the oral Torah; belief in the resurrection of the body, in angels and spirits (Acts 23:6-8); and a balance between divine providence and human free will. They extended priestly purity rules to everyday meals and tithed carefully, even garden herbs (Matt 23:23). Within the movement the schools of Hillel and Shammai debated questions such as divorce and Sabbath rules.

The gospels show sharp conflict: over Sabbath healing, purity, fasting, and Jesus' table fellowship with sinners (Mark 2:16-3:6; Mark 7:1-13). Matthew 23 contains Jesus' woes against scribes and Pharisees for hypocrisy. Yet the picture is mixed: Pharisees invite Jesus to dinner (Luke 7:36; Luke 14:1), some warn him of Herod's plot (Luke 13:31), Nicodemus seeks him out and later helps bury him (John 3:1-2; John 19:39), Gamaliel urges tolerance of the apostles (Acts 5:34-39), and some believers belonged to the party (Acts 15:5). Paul describes himself as a Pharisee, blameless as to righteousness under the law, and zealous for the ancestral traditions (Phil 3:5-6; Gal 1:14; Acts 23:6).

After AD 70, sages largely in the Pharisaic tradition regrouped at Yavneh and shaped rabbinic Judaism, the Mishnah and Talmud. Christian preaching has often caricatured Pharisees as legalists who thought they earned salvation; since E. P. Sanders' *Paul and Palestinian Judaism* (1977) many scholars describe their religion as 'covenantal nomism', obedience as response to grace within the covenant. Others argue that works still played a role in final judgment in some Jewish texts. This debate underlies the 'New Perspective on Paul' and wider discussion of justification.

title: The Sadducees
summary: The Sadducees were an aristocratic party closely tied to the high-priestly families and the temple. They rejected the Pharisees' oral traditions and denied the resurrection, and they disappear from history after the temple's fall.
body:
The name is usually connected with Zadok, Solomon's high priest, whose descendants held the high priesthood for centuries (1 Kgs 2:35; Ezek 44:15). As a party they appear in the Hasmonean period. Josephus describes them as few in number but drawn from the leading men, rough in manner even with one another, and able to win the elite but not the populace. In the first century the high-priestly families, such as that of Annas, were associated with them (Acts 5:17).

Their core principle was that only the written law was binding, not the Pharisees' ancestral traditions. Some church fathers said they accepted only the five books of Moses, but it is more likely that they rejected the oral tradition rather than the Prophets and Writings. They denied the resurrection of the body and, according to Acts, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8); Josephus adds that they denied fate and held that the soul perished with the body. Their question to Jesus about a woman married successively to seven brothers under levirate law was designed to make resurrection look absurd, and Jesus answered from the Torah itself, from God's words at the bush (Mark 12:18-27; Exod 3:6).

In Acts the Sadducees, with the high priest, arrest Peter and John because they proclaim resurrection in Jesus (Acts 4:1-3), and Paul exploits the Pharisee-Sadducee split on resurrection when he stands before the council (Acts 23:6-10). Annas, high priest AD 6-15, saw five sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas hold the office; Caiaphas served from about AD 18 to 36, a long tenure suggesting skill in working with Roman governors. An ornate ossuary inscribed 'Joseph son of Caiaphas', found in Jerusalem in 1990, probably belonged to his family.

Because their power base was the temple and its cooperation with Rome, the Sadducees did not survive the destruction of AD 70. What we know of them comes from opponents: Josephus, the New Testament and later rabbinic texts, so their own self-understanding is hard to recover. Their denial of resurrection makes them important background to the New Testament's insistence on a bodily resurrection.

title: The Essenes and Qumran
summary: The Essenes were a strict Jewish movement described by Josephus, Philo and Pliny. Most scholars link them with the community at Qumran whose library, the Dead Sea Scrolls, transformed knowledge of the Old Testament text and of Judaism in Jesus' time.
body:
Ancient writers describe the Essenes as a disciplined movement of about four thousand men living in towns across Judea, sharing property, eating communal meals after ritual bathing, wearing white, avoiding oaths and practising a long probation before full membership. Pliny the Elder places a community of Essenes on the western shore of the Dead Sea, above En-gedi (*Natural History* 5.73). The Essenes are never named in the New Testament.

From 1947 onward, Bedouin and archaeologists found the remains of some nine hundred manuscripts in eleven caves near Khirbet Qumran. About a quarter are biblical, representing every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther. The Great Isaiah Scroll, copied around 125 BC, is about a thousand years older than the medieval manuscripts on which printed Hebrew Bibles were based, and largely agrees with them, while other scrolls show textual variety, some agreeing with the Septuagint. This bears directly on discussions of how scripture was transmitted.

The sectarian scrolls describe a community led by priests, founded or shaped by a 'Teacher of Righteousness' opposed by a 'Wicked Priest', usually identified with a Hasmonean high priest. Key texts include the Community Rule, the Damascus Document, the War Scroll, the Temple Scroll, hymns, and commentaries (*pesharim*) applying prophets such as Habakkuk to their own day. They kept a 364-day solar calendar, saw themselves as the true Israel in a new covenant, and expected two messiahs, one priestly and one royal, 'of Aaron and Israel'. The settlement was destroyed by the Romans around AD 68. Most scholars identify the Qumran group with the Essenes, though some dispute the link or argue the scrolls came from Jerusalem.

The scrolls illuminate the New Testament without explaining it away. The Community Rule applies Isaiah 40:3, 'prepare the way of the Lord in the wilderness', to the community's withdrawal, the same text used of John the Baptist (Mark 1:2-4). A fragment known as 4Q521 links a messiah with healing the wounded, raising the dead and bringing good news to the poor, close to Jesus' answer to John (Matt 11:4-5). Language of 'sons of light', works of the law and a new covenant appears in both. Some have suggested John the Baptist had contact with the community; this is speculative.

title: Zealots and Revolutionaries
summary: 'Zeal' for God's law had deep roots in Israel's story, and in the first century it fed movements that resisted Roman rule, culminating in the Zealot party of the revolt of AD 66-70. One of Jesus' disciples was called Simon the Zealot.
body:
Israel's scriptures honored zeal for God's honor. Phinehas killed an Israelite and a Midianite woman in the act of idolatry and received a covenant of peace because he was 'zealous for his God' (Num 25:7-13; Ps 106:30-31). Elijah declared himself very zealous for the LORD (1 Kgs 19:10). Jehu boasted of his zeal (2 Kgs 10:16). In the Maccabean revolt Mattathias called out 'let everyone who is zealous for the law follow me' (1 Maccabees 2:27). Paul says that before his conversion he was 'extremely zealous' for the ancestral traditions and persecuted the church out of zeal (Gal 1:13-14; Phil 3:6).

In AD 6, when Judea came under direct Roman rule and a census was taken for taxation, Judas the Galilean led a revolt teaching that to pay tribute to Rome was to accept a human master in place of God (Acts 5:37). Josephus calls this the 'fourth philosophy' alongside Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes (*Antiquities* 18.23). Later the *sicarii*, 'dagger-men', assassinated collaborators in festival crowds; the Roman tribune mistook Paul for 'the Egyptian' who had led four thousand of them into the wilderness (Acts 21:38). Barabbas had been imprisoned for murder in an insurrection (Mark 15:7), and the men crucified with Jesus are called *lestai*, a word for bandits often used of insurgents (Mark 15:27).

The Zealots as a named party appear in Josephus' account of the war of AD 66-70, when they seized the temple in Jerusalem. Whether there was a continuous Zealot movement from Judas to the revolt is debated; many historians now see a cluster of different groups rather than one organization. Masada, held by sicarii under Eleazar ben Yair, fell in AD 73 or 74.

Simon, one of the Twelve, is called 'the Zealot' (Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13) and in Mark and Matthew 'the Cananaean', from the Aramaic for zealous (Mark 3:18). It is uncertain whether this means he belonged to a revolutionary group or simply had a zealous temperament. Jesus included both him and Matthew the tax collector among the Twelve, rejected armed resistance (Matt 26:52) and said his kingdom was not of this world (John 18:36), while also being executed as 'King of the Jews', a charge with political overtones.

title: The Samaritans
summary: The Samaritans were the people of the central hill country who worshipped Israel's God on Mount Gerizim and accepted only the Torah as scripture. Centuries of rivalry with Judeans made Jesus' dealings with them, and his parable of the good Samaritan, deliberately striking.
body:
Judean tradition traced the Samaritans to the foreign colonists Assyria settled in Samaria after 722 BC, who 'feared the LORD but also served their own gods' (2 Kgs 17:24-41). Samaritans themselves claim descent from the northern tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh and call themselves *Shamerim*, 'keepers' of the law. The truth likely includes both: a mixed population with a strong Israelite core. Tension appears after the exile, when the returning Judeans refused help from 'the people of the land' and Sanballat, governor of Samaria, opposed Nehemiah's walls (Ezra 4:1-5; Neh 4:1-8).

The Samaritans built a temple on Mount Gerizim above Shechem; excavations suggest a sanctuary there from the fifth century BC. John Hyrcanus destroyed it around 111-110 BC, deepening the hostility. Samaritans accepted only their own version of the five books of Moses, the Samaritan Pentateuch, which differs from the Jewish text in many small ways and in a few deliberate ones, notably naming Gerizim as the chosen place of worship. They expected a figure called the *Taheb*, 'restorer', a prophet like Moses (Deut 18:15-18).

In the gospels the hostility is plain. Jews had no dealings with Samaritans (John 4:9), a Samaritan village refused Jesus because he was heading to Jerusalem, and James and John wanted to call down fire (Luke 9:51-56). Galilean pilgrims often avoided Samaria by crossing the Jordan. Against this backdrop Jesus talks with a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well about true worship and reveals himself as the Messiah she expects (John 4:19-26), makes a Samaritan the hero of a parable about neighbor-love (Luke 10:25-37), and notes that the only healed leper to return was a Samaritan (Luke 17:11-19).

Acts portrays Samaria as the next stage of the mission after Jerusalem and Judea (Acts 1:8). Philip preaches there, Peter and John come down and the Samaritans receive the Spirit (Acts 8:4-25). In AD 36 Pilate's attack on a Samaritan crowd gathering at Gerizim led to his recall to Rome. A small Samaritan community survives today, numbering under a thousand, on Mount Gerizim and in Holon near Tel Aviv, still keeping Passover sacrifice on the mountain.
