title: Scribes
summary: Scribes began as royal secretaries and record-keepers and became, by the first century, the recognized experts in interpreting and applying the law of Moses. They were a profession rather than a party, though many were Pharisees.
body:
In a largely non-literate society, those who could write held important posts. Israel's kings had scribes who served as secretaries of state: Seraiah under David, Shaphan under Josiah, who read the rediscovered book of the law to the king (2 Sam 8:17; 2 Kgs 22:8-10). Baruch wrote Jeremiah's prophecies from dictation and recopied them after King Jehoiakim burned the scroll (Jer 36:4; Jer 36:27-32). Seal impressions (bullae) bearing names such as 'Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe' have been published, though their authenticity has been questioned.

After the exile the role shifted from administration to the law. Ezra was 'a scribe skilled in the law of Moses' who set his heart to study, do and teach it (Ezra 7:6; Ezra 7:10). At the Water Gate he read the law aloud while Levites helped the people understand, giving the sense (Neh 8:1-8), a model of public reading with interpretation. The second-century BC sage Ben Sira describes the scribe's life of leisure for study, devoted to the law, wisdom and prophecies, in contrast to farmers and craftsmen (Sirach 38:24-39:11).

In the New Testament, scribes (*grammateis*) appear as legal experts, also called lawyers and teachers of the law (Luke 5:17; Luke 11:45-52). They taught in synagogues, judged cases and sat on the Sanhedrin with chief priests and elders (Mark 14:53). Some belonged to the Pharisees (Mark 2:16), but the category was professional, not partisan. Crowds noticed that Jesus taught with authority, not as their scribes did, who taught by citing earlier authorities (Matt 7:28-29). Jesus criticized scribes who loved honor and devoured widows' houses (Mark 12:38-40), yet commended one who was 'not far from the kingdom' (Mark 12:28-34) and spoke of 'every scribe trained for the kingdom' (Matt 13:52).

Scribes also preserved scripture by copying it, with careful practices that later Masoretes developed into elaborate systems of counting letters and noting variants. In the Greco-Roman world professional secretaries (*amanuenses*) wrote letters from dictation; Tertius identifies himself as the one who wrote Romans (Rom 16:22), and Paul sometimes added a greeting in his own hand (Gal 6:11; 2 Thess 3:17).

title: The Sanhedrin
summary: The Sanhedrin was Jerusalem's supreme Jewish council of chief priests, elders and scribes, presided over by the high priest under Roman oversight. It examined Jesus, tried the apostles and heard Paul.
body:
The word comes from Greek *synedrion*, 'sitting together', a council. Later rabbinic tradition describes a Great Sanhedrin of seventy-one members modeled on the seventy elders who assisted Moses (Num 11:16-17; Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:6), with smaller courts of twenty-three in towns. The New Testament and Josephus, closer in time, present a council of chief priests, elders and scribes convened and led by the ruling high priest (Mark 14:53; Mark 15:1; Acts 5:21). How fixed its membership and procedures were in the first century is debated; it may have been more of an advisory body summoned by the high priest than a standing court.

Under Roman rule the council handled internal religious and civil matters for Judea and controlled the temple police, who arrested Jesus and the apostles (John 18:3; Acts 5:24-26). Capital punishment, however, was reserved to the Roman governor: 'it is not lawful for us to put anyone to death' (John 18:31). Stephen's stoning appears to be a lynching rather than a lawful sentence (Acts 7:57-58), and Josephus reports that when the high priest Ananus had James the brother of Jesus stoned in AD 62, during a gap between governors, he was removed from office (*Antiquities* 20.200-203).

The gospels describe a night hearing at Caiaphas' house and a morning consultation before Jesus was handed to Pilate (Mark 14:53-65; Mark 15:1). The Mishnah's later rules forbid capital trials at night, on a festival or its eve, and require a day's delay before conviction, so some argue the proceedings were illegal; others reply that the Mishnah may describe idealized or later practice, or that the hearing was a preliminary inquiry. Not all members agreed: Nicodemus protested that the law does not judge a man without hearing him (John 7:50-51), and Joseph of Arimathea had not consented (Luke 23:50-51).

In Acts the council threatens and flogs Peter and John (Acts 4:5-21; Acts 5:27-40), where the Pharisee Gamaliel's counsel of caution prevails, tries Stephen (Acts 6:12-15), and hears Paul, who divides it by appealing to the resurrection (Acts 22:30-23:10). After AD 70 the Jerusalem Sanhedrin ceased; rabbinic courts at Yavneh and later in Galilee claimed its succession.

title: Messianic Expectations
summary: Jews of Jesus' day held a range of hopes for God's coming deliverance: a royal son of David, a priestly messiah, a prophet like Moses, a returning Elijah, or a heavenly Son of Man. There was no single, uniform expectation, which helps explain the debates about Jesus' identity.
body:
'Messiah' (Hebrew *mashiach*, Greek *christos*) means 'anointed'. In the Old Testament kings were anointed (1 Sam 16:13; 1 Sam 24:6), as were priests (Lev 4:3), and Isaiah even calls the Persian Cyrus the LORD's anointed (Isa 45:1). The central messianic hope grew from God's promise to David of an everlasting dynasty (2 Sam 7:12-16). After the monarchy failed, prophets looked for a righteous branch from Jesse's stump, a ruler from Bethlehem, a restored booth of David (Isa 9:6-7; Isa 11:1-10; Jer 23:5-6; Mic 5:2; Amos 9:11).

Second Temple texts show variety. The *Psalms of Solomon* (17), written after Pompey's conquest, pray for a son of David to purge Jerusalem of Gentiles and rule in righteousness. The Qumran scrolls expect both a royal messiah of Israel and a priestly messiah of Aaron. Others waited for the prophet like Moses (Deut 18:15-18) or for Elijah before the day of the LORD (Mal 4:5-6), which is why John the Baptist was asked whether he was the Christ, Elijah or the Prophet (John 1:19-25). Daniel's 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds to receive dominion (Dan 7:13-14) was developed in *1 Enoch* into a pre-existent heavenly judge. The suffering servant of Isaiah 52-53 was not, so far as surviving evidence shows, widely read as a dying messiah before Christianity, though this is debated.

Several would-be kings and prophets arose: after Herod's death in 4 BC men named Judas, Simon and Athronges claimed royal power; Theudas promised to part the Jordan (Acts 5:36); an Egyptian prophet led followers to the Mount of Olives (Acts 21:38). In AD 132 Simon bar Kosiba led a revolt and was hailed by Rabbi Akiva as 'Bar Kokhba', 'son of the star', alluding to Numbers 24:17. All ended in Roman defeat.

Against this background Jesus was cautious with the title. When Peter confessed him as the Christ, he spoke at once of the Son of Man suffering (Mark 8:27-33); he withdrew when crowds wanted to make him king (John 6:15); and he redefined kingship through his entry on a donkey (Zech 9:9; Matt 21:1-11) and his death. Simeon and Anna in the temple represent pious hope for the consolation and redemption of Israel (Luke 2:25-38). How the Old Testament hopes are fulfilled in Jesus, and whether some await a future earthly fulfilment for Israel, is debated among Christians.

title: Diaspora Judaism
summary: By the first century most Jews lived outside the land of Israel, in communities from Babylon to Rome. These Greek-speaking synagogues were the bridge by which the gospel reached the Gentile world.
body:
The dispersion (Greek *diaspora*) began with the Assyrian and Babylonian deportations and grew through voluntary migration for trade and military service. Jews served as soldiers at Elephantine in Egypt under Persia, and under the Ptolemies and Seleucids large communities formed in Alexandria, Antioch and Asia Minor. Philo says Jews occupied two of Alexandria's five districts. Estimates of the total Jewish population in the first century vary widely, but most agree that more lived outside Judea than within it. The list of pilgrims at Pentecost, from Parthia and Mesopotamia to Rome, Crete and Arabia, reflects this spread (Acts 2:5-11).

Diaspora Jews kept their identity through Sabbath, circumcision, food laws, synagogues and the annual temple tax sent to Jerusalem. Julius Caesar and Augustus granted privileges: freedom to assemble, to keep the Sabbath and to send money to the temple, and exemption from military service. They read the scriptures in Greek, the Septuagint, and produced literature in Greek, including the works of Philo of Alexandria, who interpreted Moses through Platonic philosophy. Many Gentiles were attracted as 'God-fearers' who attended synagogue without full conversion (Acts 10:2; Acts 13:16), and some became proselytes (Acts 2:10; Acts 6:5).

The New Testament is full of diaspora Jews. Paul was born in Tarsus and was a Roman citizen (Acts 22:3; Acts 22:28); Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus (Acts 4:36); Apollos was an eloquent Alexandrian (Acts 18:24); Timothy had a Jewish mother and a Greek father (Acts 16:1). Claudius expelled Jews from Rome around AD 49, which brought Priscilla and Aquila to Corinth (Acts 18:2); the Roman historian Suetonius links the expulsion to disturbances over 'Chrestus', perhaps a garbled reference to Christ. Jesus' opponents wondered if he would go to 'the dispersion among the Greeks' (John 7:35).

James and 1 Peter are addressed to the dispersion, applying the term to the church as God's scattered people (Jas 1:1; 1 Pet 1:1). Paul's mission strategy went first to the synagogue in each city (Acts 13:5; Acts 14:1), and the tension over Gentile inclusion without circumcision was largely a diaspora question. Esther and Daniel had already shown faithful Jews living in a foreign empire (Esth 4:14; Dan 6:10).

title: Greco-Roman Religion and Mystery Cults
summary: The religious world of Paul's churches was crowded with civic gods, household spirits, healing shrines, oracles, magic and initiatory 'mystery' cults. Conversion to Christ meant leaving much of this daily practice behind.
body:
Greek and Roman religion was civic and practical rather than creedal. Each city honored its gods with temples, festivals, processions and sacrifices, on the principle of reciprocity, 'I give so that you may give'. Priests were often civic officials, and piety meant performing rites correctly rather than holding particular beliefs. Households honored their own protective spirits, the Roman *lares* and *penates*, at small shrines. Because sacrifice was woven into guild banquets, civic festivals and the meat market, Christians in Corinth had to ask whether they could eat food offered to idols (1 Cor 8:1-13; 1 Cor 10:14-30).

Acts shows this world vividly. At Lystra the crowd hails Barnabas as Zeus and Paul as Hermes, recalling a local legend of the gods visiting in human form, and the priest of Zeus brings oxen to sacrifice (Acts 14:8-18). In Athens Paul finds an altar 'to an unknown god' (Acts 17:23). At Ephesus, home of the great temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the world, silversmiths riot when the gospel threatens their trade in shrines (Acts 19:23-41), and new believers burn magic books worth 50,000 silver drachmas (Acts 19:19). A slave girl at Philippi has a 'python spirit', linked with the Delphic oracle (Acts 16:16-18), and Paul's last ship bears the figurehead of the Twin Brothers, Castor and Pollux, protectors of sailors (Acts 28:11). Healing shrines of Asclepius, such as those at Corinth and Pergamum, drew the sick.

The mystery religions offered something more personal: secret initiation into the story of a deity, promising blessing in this life and a better lot after death. The oldest were the Eleusinian mysteries of Demeter and Persephone near Athens. Others honored Dionysus, Isis and Osiris (described in Apuleius' *Metamorphoses* book 11), and Cybele and Attis. The cult of Mithras as practised in the Roman army flourished mostly from the late first century to the fourth. Their rites were secret, so much of what we know is fragmentary and late.

In the early twentieth century the 'history of religions' school argued that Paul's teaching on baptism and the Lord's Supper borrowed from these cults' dying-and-rising gods and sacred meals. Critics point out that most evidence for the cults' parallels dates after the New Testament, that the myths are seasonal rather than historical, and that Paul's language is rooted in Jewish categories such as Passover and covenant (1 Cor 5:7; 1 Cor 11:23-26). Most scholars now see shared vocabulary rather than borrowing, though the conversation continues. Paul's warning against sharing the table of the Lord and the table of demons (1 Cor 10:20-21) shows that he saw the two as rivals, not cousins.

title: The Imperial Cult
summary: Across the Roman East, cities honored the emperor with temples, priests, sacrifices and festivals as a divine savior and lord. Christian confession of Jesus as Lord and Son of God sounded, in this setting, like a rival allegiance.
body:
After Julius Caesar was officially deified in 42 BC, his adopted son Octavian, later Augustus, took the title *divi filius*, 'son of the divine one'. In Rome emperors were usually deified only after death, but in the Greek East living emperors received worship as gods from the start: Augustus permitted temples to Rome and himself at Pergamum and Nicomedia in 29 BC. Emperor worship was promoted not mainly by emperors but by provincial elites eager to show loyalty, and it was woven into civic life through festivals, games, statues and oaths.

The language of this cult overlapped with the gospel's. A famous inscription from Priene (9 BC), adopting Augustus' birthday as the start of the provincial year, praises him as a savior who ended war and says his birthday was the beginning of 'good news' (*euangelia*) for the world. Emperors were called savior (*soter*), lord (*kyrios*), and son of god. Against this backdrop, Paul's proclamation of Jesus as Lord, before whom every knee will bow, and of a Savior from heaven (Phil 2:9-11; Phil 3:20), and the charge at Thessalonica that Christians said 'there is another king, Jesus' (Acts 17:7), carried political force. Some scholars argue Paul deliberately countered imperial ideology; others think the overlap is less intentional.

In the province of Asia, cities competed to be 'temple-keepers' (*neokoroi*) of the emperor's cult: Pergamum, with its early temple to Augustus; Smyrna, awarded a temple to Tiberius in AD 26; and Ephesus, which built a temple of the Flavian emperors around AD 89/90 under Domitian. These are among the seven churches of Revelation (Rev 2:1-17). 'Satan's throne' at Pergamum (Rev 2:13) may refer to the imperial cult, and Revelation's beast that demands worship of its image and controls buying and selling (Rev 13:4-17) is widely read against emperor worship.

Early in the second century Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia, tested accused Christians by asking them to offer incense and wine to the emperor's image and curse Christ, executing those who refused (*Letters* 10.96). The account of Polycarp's martyrdom has the magistrate urging him to say 'Caesar is Lord'. Thomas' confession 'my Lord and my God' (John 20:28) and the Christian refusal to offer even a pinch of incense show how exclusive confession of Christ collided with imperial religion.

title: Stoicism and Epicureanism
summary: Stoics and Epicureans were the two most influential philosophical schools of the New Testament era, offering rival accounts of the gods, the world and the good life. Paul met both in Athens, and their vocabulary echoes in the letters.
body:
Stoicism was founded by Zeno of Citium, who taught at the Painted Stoa in Athens around 300 BC. Stoics held that the universe is a single rational whole pervaded by divine reason (*logos*), sometimes called Zeus or God or Nature. The wise person lives 'according to nature', regards virtue as the only true good, and is indifferent to wealth, health and status, achieving freedom from destructive passions. Stoics believed in providence and a cyclical conflagration and renewal of the cosmos. In Paul's time leading Stoics included Seneca, Nero's tutor and the brother of Gallio, proconsul of Achaia (Acts 18:12-17), and slightly later Epictetus, a former slave whose *Discourses* were recorded by a student.

Epicureanism was founded by Epicurus (341-270 BC), who taught in his Garden at Athens. The world is made of atoms moving in a void; the gods exist but live in blissful detachment and do not intervene; the soul dissolves at death, so 'death is nothing to us'. The goal of life is pleasure, understood as tranquillity (*ataraxia*) and absence of pain, best found in simple living and friendship. The Roman poet Lucretius set out the system in *On the Nature of Things*. Opponents caricatured it as 'eat, drink and be merry', and Paul quotes Isaiah's version of that motto against those who deny resurrection (1 Cor 15:32; Isa 22:13).

In Athens Epicurean and Stoic philosophers debated with Paul and brought him to the Areopagus (Acts 17:18-19). His speech engages both: against Epicureans, God made the world and is near to every person; with Stoics, God needs nothing and gives life and breath; he quotes 'we are his offspring', from the Stoic-influenced poet Aratus (Acts 17:24-28). But his call to repentance before a fixed day of judgment by a man raised from the dead offended both schools (Acts 17:30-32).

Scholars note Stoic echoes elsewhere: Paul's contentment (*autarkes*, a Stoic ideal) in all circumstances, grounded in Christ's strength rather than self-sufficiency (Phil 4:11-13); the role of conscience (Rom 2:14-15); and lists of virtues and vices (Gal 5:19-23). John's *logos* (John 1:1-14) has been linked to Stoic and to Philo's usage, though most see its primary roots in the Old Testament word and wisdom of God (Gen 1:3; Ps 33:6; Prov 8:22-31). How far biblical writers borrowed from philosophy, and how far they confronted it, is part of the wider question of revelation and culture.

title: Roads, Travel and Travel Times
summary: Roman roads, sea lanes and a century of relative peace made travel easier than ever before, though it remained slow, costly and dangerous. Knowing typical distances and speeds brings biblical journeys down to earth.
body:
Rome built a network of some 80,000 km of main paved roads, with milestones every Roman mile (about 1,480 m). In Paul's world the Via Egnatia, built in the second century BC, ran across Macedonia through Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia and Thessalonica, exactly the route of Acts 17:1. The Via Appia brought Paul to Rome, where believers met him at the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns (Acts 28:15). The imperial courier service could average around 75 km a day using relays of horses, but ordinary people walked. A traveler on foot typically covered 25-30 km (15-20 miles) a day; a loaded donkey or caravan moved at about the same pace or slower.

Sea travel was faster with a fair wind and could cover 100-150 km a day, but it was seasonal. Sailing was considered dangerous from mid-September and largely suspended from about November to March; Paul's voyage was risky because 'the Fast', the Day of Atonement, was already past (Acts 27:9). Alexandrian grain ships, large enough to carry 276 people (Acts 27:37), could reach Rome in two to three weeks but took much longer on the return against prevailing winds. Travelers faced shipwreck, bandits, rivers and exposure, as Paul's catalogue of dangers shows (2 Cor 11:25-27), and stayed with hosts or in inns of poor reputation (Luke 10:34).

Some biblical travel times, using these rates: Ezra's party took about four months to travel from Babylon to Jerusalem, leaving on the first day of the first month and arriving on the first day of the fifth (Ezra 7:8-9). Deuteronomy notes it is eleven days from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea by the Mount Seir road (Deut 1:2). Nazareth to Bethlehem is about 150 km, perhaps four to seven days for Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:4-5). Galilee to Jerusalem was roughly 120-150 km, three to five days, by the Jordan valley route or directly through Samaria (Luke 9:51-53; John 4:3-4). Jerusalem to Jericho is about 27 km with a descent of roughly 1,000 m, the steep, lonely road of the good Samaritan (Luke 10:30). Emmaus was 60 stadia, about 11 km, from Jerusalem (Luke 24:13), and a Sabbath day's journey about 1 km (Acts 1:12).

Paul's journeys, adding land and sea, are often estimated at well over 10,000 km, though such figures depend on reconstructing his routes. His letters were carried by co-workers such as Phoebe, Tychicus and Epaphroditus (Rom 16:1-2; Col 4:7-8; Phil 2:25), and churches sent people back and forth with news and gifts, creating a network that made a scattered movement feel like one body.

title: Food and Meals
summary: Most people ate a simple diet built on bread, olive oil and wine, with vegetables, legumes, fruit and occasional fish or meat. Meals were also social events that marked status and belonging, which is why Jesus' table fellowship mattered so much.
body:
The Mediterranean staples were grain, new wine and oil (Deut 7:13; Ps 104:14-15). Bread supplied perhaps half or more of an ordinary person's calories, so 'daily bread' was no metaphor (Matt 6:11). Wheat bread was preferred; barley was cheaper and associated with the poor, as with the boy's five barley loaves (John 6:9). Revelation's famine price, a quart of wheat for a denarius or three of barley, implies roughly a day's wage for one person's daily bread (Rev 6:6). Women ground grain each day by hand mill (Matt 24:41) and baked in household or shared ovens.

Alongside bread came lentils and beans (Gen 25:34; Ezek 4:9), onions, leeks and garlic (Num 11:5), olives, figs, grapes, dates and pomegranates, cheese, curds and honey. Around the Sea of Galilee fish were dried or salted for trade; Magdala's Greek name, Taricheae, probably refers to fish-salting. Meat was costly and reserved for festivals, sacrifices and guests, which is why killing the fatted calf signalled extravagant celebration (Luke 15:23). Wine was the normal drink, usually diluted with water, and John the Baptist's diet of locusts and wild honey marked him as a wilderness figure (Mark 1:6).

Ordinary people ate a light morning meal and a main meal in the evening. At formal dinners, following Greco-Roman custom, guests reclined on couches around low tables, leaning on the left elbow with feet extended away from the table. This explains how a woman could stand behind Jesus at his feet and wash them (Luke 7:37-38) and how the beloved disciple could lean back against Jesus' chest (John 13:23-25). Places reflected rank (Luke 14:7-11), and the host's choice of guests displayed his social circle (Luke 14:12-14).

Because eating together signalled acceptance, Jesus' meals with tax collectors and sinners drew criticism (Mark 2:15-17; Luke 15:1-2), and table fellowship between Jews and Gentiles became the crisis at Antioch (Gal 2:11-14). Early Christians ate the Lord's Supper as part of a full meal in homes, and Paul rebukes the Corinthians because wealthier members ate and drank while poorer ones went hungry (1 Cor 11:17-34). Scripture's hope is pictured as a feast: rich food and aged wine on God's mountain, many coming from east and west to recline with Abraham, and the marriage supper of the Lamb (Isa 25:6-8; Matt 8:11; Rev 19:9).

title: Houses and Clothing
summary: Most biblical-era families lived in small stone or mud-brick houses grouped around shared courtyards, with flat roofs used as living space. Clothing was simple, a tunic and a cloak, and many laws and sayings assume its details.
body:
The typical Iron Age Israelite dwelling was the 'four-room' or pillared house: a central open or roofed space flanked by rows of pillars, side rooms for animals and storage, and a broad room at the back. Livestock were stabled on the ground floor and the family lived and slept largely upstairs or on the roof. Roofs were flat, made of beams covered with branches and packed clay, and were used for drying produce, sleeping and prayer, so the law required a parapet (Deut 22:8). Rahab hid the spies among flax on her roof (Josh 2:6), Samuel spoke with Saul on a roof (1 Sam 9:25-26), and Peter prayed on one in Joppa (Acts 10:9).

In first-century Galilean villages such as Capernaum, houses were built of local basalt with roofs of beams and clay, grouped in blocks of rooms around shared courtyards where related families cooked and worked. Friends of a paralytic could dig through such a roof to lower him down (Mark 2:4); Luke, writing for readers used to tiled roofs, mentions tiles (Luke 5:19). One room at Capernaum was venerated by Christians as Peter's house from an early date and later enclosed by an octagonal church. Many homes had a guest room or upper room (*katalyma*), the word used for the room of the Last Supper (Luke 22:11-12) and, many scholars argue, in Luke 2:7, suggesting Jesus was laid in the animals' area of a crowded family house rather than turned away from a commercial inn.

In cities, the poor lived in multi-storey apartment blocks (*insulae*) with shops on the ground floor; Eutychus fell from a third-storey window (Acts 20:9). The wealthy lived in a *domus* arranged around an atrium and dining room. The earliest churches met in houses, such as those of Priscilla and Aquila, Nympha and Philemon (Rom 16:5; Col 4:15; Phlm 1:2), which limited a congregation to perhaps a few dozen people. The oldest securely identified house church, at Dura-Europos in Syria, dates from the 230s-250s.

Clothing was basic. Men and women wore a tunic (Hebrew *kuttonet*, Greek *chiton*) of wool or linen and an outer cloak (*simlah*, *himation*) that doubled as a blanket; if taken in pledge it had to be returned by night (Exod 22:26-27; Deut 24:12-13). Jesus' teaching on giving the cloak as well as the tunic assumes these two garments (Matt 5:40), and soldiers gambled for his seamless tunic (John 19:23-24). Israelite men wore tassels on the corners of their cloaks (Num 15:37-41; Matt 9:20), the pious wore phylacteries (Matt 23:5), and wool and linen were not to be mixed (Deut 22:11). Purple dye from murex shellfish was a luxury, the trade of Lydia (Acts 16:14) and the mark of the rich man (Luke 16:19). People 'girded their loins' by tucking the tunic into a belt for work or running (1 Kgs 18:46; Luke 12:35), and tore their clothes or wore sackcloth in grief (Gen 37:34).

title: Money, Weights and Measures
summary: Before coinage, silver was weighed in shekels; by the New Testament era Roman, Greek and Jewish coins circulated side by side. Converting biblical sums and measures into everyday terms reveals the force of many texts.
body:
For most of the Old Testament period there were no coins. Silver and gold were weighed on balances using stone weights, and 'shekel' was a unit of weight, about 11.4 g in Judah on the evidence of inscribed weights. Abraham weighed out 400 shekels of silver for the cave of Machpelah (Gen 23:16), and Jeremiah weighed 17 shekels for a field at Anathoth (Jer 32:9-10). Fifty shekels made a mina (Ezekiel gives sixty) and a talent was 3,000 shekels, about 34 kg (Exod 38:25-26; Ezek 45:12). Dishonest merchants kept two sets of weights, which the prophets condemned (Amos 8:5; Prov 11:1). Coinage, invented in Lydia in the seventh century BC, reached Judah under Persia: the gold daric appears in Ezra and Nehemiah (Ezra 2:69; Neh 7:70-72), and small silver 'Yehud' coins were minted in the fourth century.

In Jesus' day the denarius, a Roman silver coin of about 3.9 g, was a day's wage for a laborer (Matt 20:2). The Greek drachma was roughly equal (Luke 15:8). The temple tax of two drachmas was the didrachma (Matt 17:24), and a stater or tetradrachm, in practice the Tyrian shekel, paid it for two people (Matt 17:27). The thirty pieces of silver paid to Judas were probably Tyrian shekels, echoing the price of a slave and Zechariah's prophecy (Matt 26:15; Exod 21:32; Zech 11:12-13). Small bronze coins included the assarion, a sixteenth of a denarius, for which two sparrows were sold (Matt 10:29), and the lepton, the smallest Jewish coin; the widow's two lepta made a quadrans, a sixty-fourth of a denarius (Mark 12:42).

Larger sums: a mina was 100 drachmas, about four months' wages (Luke 19:13); a talent was 6,000 denarii, some twenty years' wages for a laborer. The servant forgiven 10,000 talents, an unpayable sum of about sixty million denarii, refuses to forgive a debt of 100 denarii (Matt 18:24-28). Mary's nard was worth over 300 denarii, a year's wages (Mark 14:5; John 12:5), Philip reckoned 200 denarii would not feed the five thousand (John 6:7), and the good Samaritan left two denarii, about two days' wages, for the innkeeper (Luke 10:35).

Length was measured by the body: the cubit, elbow to fingertip, about 44.5 cm (a longer royal cubit was about 52 cm), the span (half a cubit), the handbreadth and the finger. Noah's ark measured 300 by 50 by 30 cubits (Gen 6:15) and Goliath six cubits and a span, about 2.9 m (1 Sam 17:4). The Greek stadion was about 185 m (Luke 24:13), the Roman mile about 1,480 m (Matt 5:41), and the fathom about 1.85 m (Acts 27:28). Dry measures included the ephah, perhaps 22 liters though estimates vary, the omer, a tenth of an ephah (Exod 16:36), and the homer of ten ephahs (Ezek 45:11). The bath, a liquid measure equal to the ephah, and the hin and log measured oil and wine. The stone jars at Cana held two or three measures each, perhaps 80-120 liters (John 2:6).

title: Agriculture and the Seasons
summary: Most people in Israel lived by farming grain, vines and olives under a climate of winter rains and dry summers. The agricultural year shaped the festivals, the prophets' imagery and Jesus' parables.
body:
Israel has two seasons: a rainy winter and a dry summer. The 'early rain' (*yoreh*) in October and November softened the ground for ploughing and sowing; winter rains followed; the 'latter rain' (*malqosh*) in March and April filled out the grain before harvest (Deut 11:14; Joel 2:23; Jas 5:7). From May to September there was virtually no rain, and summer crops depended on heavy dew (Hos 14:5). Unlike Egypt with its Nile, the land 'drinks water by the rain from heaven', which made Israel's farmers dependent on God's provision and vulnerable to drought as covenant curse (Deut 11:10-17; 1 Kgs 17:1).

The Gezer calendar, a schoolboy's limestone tablet from about the tenth century BC, lists the farming year: two months of ingathering (olives), two of sowing grain, two of late sowing, a month of hoeing flax, a month of barley harvest, a month of harvest and measuring (wheat), two months of vine tending, and a month of summer fruit. Barley ripened around Passover in April (Ruth 1:22) and wheat around Pentecost in May-June; grapes were picked in late summer and olives in autumn, around the Feast of Booths. Figs ripened in early summer and late summer; Mark notes that when Jesus cursed the fig tree 'it was not the season for figs' (Mark 11:13).

Grain was cut with sickles, carried to a threshing floor where oxen or sledges trampled it (Deut 25:4; 1 Cor 9:9), and winnowed by tossing it into the evening breeze with a fork so the chaff blew away (Ruth 3:2; Ps 1:4; Matt 3:12). Gideon threshed wheat in a winepress to hide it from raiders (Judg 6:11). David bought Araunah's threshing floor, later the temple site (2 Sam 24:18-25). Elisha was ploughing with twelve yoke of oxen when Elijah called him (1 Kgs 19:19). Reapers left corners and gleanings for the poor (Lev 19:9-10). Normal yields were perhaps five to ten times the seed, so harvests of thirty, sixty and a hundredfold were extraordinary (Gen 26:12; Mark 4:8).

Vineyards required terraces, a hedge, a watchtower and a winepress, and Isaiah's song of the vineyard uses each detail (Isa 5:1-7), as does Jesus' parable of the tenants, which reflects absentee landowners and tenant farmers common in first-century Galilee (Mark 12:1-12). Olives were crushed in presses; the name Gethsemane probably means 'oil press' (Mark 14:32). Amos was a herdsman and dresser of sycamore figs (Amos 7:14). The land was to rest every seventh year (Lev 25:3-4). Jesus drew constantly on this world: sowing on different soils, mustard seed, weeds among wheat, fields white for harvest (Mark 4:3-32; Matt 13:24-30; John 4:35).

title: Medicine and Disease
summary: Ancient people faced high infant mortality, chronic infections, parasites and eye disease, with limited medical help. Healing stories in scripture, and the place of physicians, make most sense against this background.
body:
Life expectancy at birth in the Roman world was perhaps twenty to thirty years, mainly because so many infants and children died; those who reached adulthood often lived into their fifties or sixties, and the psalmist's seventy or eighty years was a full life (Ps 90:10). Common afflictions included malaria, tuberculosis, dysentery and other gut infections, intestinal parasites, which have been identified in ancient Jerusalem latrines, and eye diseases such as trachoma that left many blind. Disability usually meant poverty and begging (Mark 10:46; John 9:8; Acts 3:2).

The 'leprosy' of the Bible (Hebrew *tsara'at*, Greek *lepra*) covered a range of skin conditions, and even mold in garments and houses, defined by visible symptoms and ritual impurity (Lev 13-14). It was not limited to Hansen's disease, though DNA from a first-century burial shroud in a tomb near Jerusalem has shown that true leprosy was present. Sufferers lived outside the camp or town (Lev 13:45-46; Luke 17:12), which made Jesus' touching a leper striking (Mark 1:40-42). Naaman's healing in the Jordan shows how foreign the condition's cure was to normal means (2 Kgs 5:1-14).

Remedies included olive oil and wine on wounds (Luke 10:34; Isa 1:6), balm from Gilead (Jer 8:22), a poultice of figs on Hezekiah's boil (2 Kgs 20:7), and a little wine for the stomach (1 Tim 5:23). Saliva was thought to have healing power, and Jesus sometimes used it (Mark 8:23; John 9:6). Greek medicine in the Hippocratic tradition was practised by trained physicians, often slaves or freedmen, and Luke is called 'the beloved physician' (Col 4:14). Physicians could be costly and unsuccessful, as the woman who spent all she had and only grew worse shows (Mark 5:26). The Chronicler criticizes Asa for seeking physicians rather than the LORD (2 Chr 16:12), while Ben Sira honors physicians as God's provision.

The sick also sought gods. Shrines of Asclepius, the Greek god of healing, flourished at Pergamum, Corinth and elsewhere, with patients sleeping in the sanctuary hoping for a cure, and some scholars connect the pool of Bethesda with such healing practices (John 5:2-9). Many assumed that illness was punishment for sin, a view Job's story and Jesus both resist (John 9:1-3), though scripture also links some sickness with sin (John 5:14; 1 Cor 11:30). The gospels distinguish illness from demon possession while recording both (Mark 1:32-34). James instructs the sick to call the elders for prayer and anointing with oil (Jas 5:14-16). Whether miraculous healing continues today is part of the cessationism debate.

title: Education and Literacy
summary: Only a minority in the ancient world could read and write fluently, but teaching through the family, the synagogue and memorization meant that many knew scripture well. Greek education produced the rhetorical skills visible in the New Testament letters.
body:
Scholars distinguish several levels of literacy: recognizing letters, signing one's name, reading simple texts, and composing or copying at length. William Harris' influential study (*Ancient Literacy*, 1989) estimated that only about 10-15 percent of people in the Roman empire could read and write at a functional level, and Catherine Hezser suggested still lower figures for Jews in Roman Palestine. Others argue that Jewish emphasis on Torah reading raised literacy among men, at least for reading scripture aloud. The question is debated, but in any case most people learned by hearing.

In ancient Israel teaching began at home: parents were to impress the commands on their children, talk of them at home and on the road, and write them on doorposts (Deut 6:6-9; Prov 1:8). Abecedaries, alphabet practice texts, have been found at Izbet Sartah and Tel Zayit, and the tenth-century Gezer calendar may be a writing exercise. In one of the Lachish letters from about 588 BC an officer indignantly insists he can read a letter himself. Professional scribes handled royal and legal documents (Jer 32:10-12). Later rabbinic tradition credits Simeon ben Shetah and the high priest Joshua ben Gamla with founding schools for children, though the reliability of these reports is debated.

In the first century, synagogues were centers of instruction, and memorization was central: students learned large blocks of text by heart and teachers taught in memorable forms such as parallelism and parables. Jesus could read the Isaiah scroll in the synagogue (Luke 4:16-20), yet people asked how he had learning without having studied, meaning formal training under a rabbi (John 7:15). The council saw Peter and John as 'uneducated, common men', meaning without scribal training (Acts 4:13). Paul was educated 'at the feet of Gamaliel' in Jerusalem (Acts 22:3), and Timothy knew the scriptures from childhood through his mother and grandmother (2 Tim 1:5; 2 Tim 3:15).

Greek education moved from the elementary teacher (reading, writing, arithmetic) to the *grammaticus* (literature, especially Homer) to the rhetor (persuasive speech). A slave *paidagogos* escorted and supervised boys, an image Paul uses for the law (Gal 3:24-25). Paul's letters use rhetorical forms, though critics said his speech was unimpressive (2 Cor 10:10). Since most could not read, letters were read aloud to congregations (Col 4:16; 1 Thess 5:27), and Revelation blesses 'the one who reads aloud' and those who hear (Rev 1:3). Paul asks for his books and parchments (2 Tim 4:13).

title: Death and Burial
summary: Jews buried their dead quickly, in family tombs, with mourning rituals that lasted days or weeks; in the late Second Temple period bones were later gathered into ossuaries. These customs shape the narratives of Lazarus and of Jesus' burial and resurrection.
body:
Burial normally took place the same day as death, both because of the climate and because corpses caused impurity (Num 19:11-16; Acts 5:6-10). Israelites were buried in family tombs, and to be 'gathered to one's people' or 'to sleep with one's fathers' reflected this (Gen 25:8; 1 Kgs 2:10). Abraham's purchase of the cave of Machpelah gave his family a burial place in the land, where Sarah, Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah and Jacob were laid (Gen 23:17-20; Gen 49:29-32). Iron Age Judean tombs were rock-cut chambers with benches on which bodies were laid; later, bones were moved to a repository to make room. Two tiny silver amulets from a tomb at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem, from around 600 BC, carry the priestly blessing and are the oldest known texts of a biblical passage (Num 6:24-26).

In the late Second Temple period wealthier Jerusalem families used rock-cut tombs with long niches (*kokhim*) or arched benches. The body was washed, anointed with spices and wrapped in linen (John 19:39-40; Acts 9:37); Nicodemus brought about a hundred Roman pounds, roughly 33 kg, of myrrh and aloes, a royal quantity. About a year later the bones were gathered into a stone box called an ossuary, a practice common from about 20 BC to AD 70; ossuaries inscribed with names such as Caiaphas have been found. Tombs were sealed with stones; large round rolling stones like the one in the gospels were relatively rare and mostly used for wealthy tombs (Mark 15:46; Mark 16:3-4). Tombs were whitewashed before Passover so pilgrims would avoid impurity, the image behind Jesus' 'whitewashed tombs' (Matt 23:27).

Mourning was loud and public. Mourners tore their clothes, wore sackcloth, put dust or ashes on their heads and fasted (Gen 37:34; 2 Sam 1:11-12). Families hired professional mourning women and flute players (Jer 9:17-18; Matt 9:23). An intense mourning period lasted seven days (Gen 50:10), with a longer thirty days for great figures like Moses (Deut 34:8). Friends came to comfort the bereaved, as at Bethany (John 11:19). Lazarus had been in the tomb four days, past any doubt that he was dead (John 11:17; John 11:39).

Romans practised both cremation, dominant in the first century, and inhumation, which became standard by the late second century; poorer people joined burial clubs that paid for funerals and niches in shared tombs. Christians, following Jewish practice and their hope of resurrection, buried their dead, and from the late second century began using underground catacombs around Rome. The New Testament describes death as sleep for believers and grounds hope in Christ's bodily resurrection (1 Thess 4:13-18; 1 Cor 15:20-23; 1 Cor 15:42-44). The site of Jesus' tomb is traditionally the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, which has strong early tradition; the Garden Tomb, proposed in the nineteenth century, is an Iron Age tomb and less likely historically.
